FASHIONS OF TO-DA.

There are doubtless many of us wto are the lucky possessors of some grey squirrel back tuch as was used some ten or twelve years ago for the lining of the black cashmere cloaks which were then fashionable.

For years, this pretty fur has been considered of little account but without rhyme or reason, Madame la Mode has this season condescended to smile thereon with the result that the price of this fur has advanced considerably. The smartest looking little coats are made of grey squirrel back the dull tones of the fur enhanced by a fanciful belt or a deep collar of some coarse make of lace. Another pretty form in which this fur is used as an adjunct of dress is an empire scarf quite two yards and a

quarter in length, lined with some rich brocade of exactly the same tone as the fur. The width of this scarf or stole tie is about fourteen inches and it can be worn either low about the shoulders in the correct empire styl€ or as a long tie of the variety familiar to most of us this season.

A scarf or tie such as I have described com- pletes the smart costume depicted which is made of dark crimson frieze cut on the latest and most approved lines. The coat in thi, instance finishes in a stitched black satin waistband and is devoid of the 13:Istine which in one form or another plays such a prominent part in this season's toile: tes. The basque, however, should not be worn by by any one at all inclined to embonpolnt as it increases the width of the figure below the waist to a considerable degree.

Some of the latest costumes have a basque long as to give very much the appearance of an over skirt. In ne.,rlv every instance the basque is detachable while a cap 3 is very often arranged in the same manner. The charm of these easily donned and dolled item- lies in the fact that one good well made gown can be induced thereby to take on variou- presentiments and in this wise do duty for several.

When worn indoors, a pretty chemisette awl dainty collar and cuffs soften the plain lines of the tailor made while opt of doors the ape and basque add to the warmth of the toilette and give a smart finish, which is increased by the addition of some fur article such as a stole tie or empire scarf in one or other of the most fashionable furs,
I must confess that the fashion for wearing 4he iur wrap draped round the shoulders or
11E HAT,
falling loosely- round the figure appears to me absurd, as the throlt and chest are left exposed and colds mad coughs seem a natural conse- quence. . .

The .charmingly picturesque hat sketched is formed of ivory tinted beaver with a crown of some furry material caught round with a band of emerald green velvet rittbon, the same ribbon forming rue velvet, flower:, which cover the bandeau while a creamy ostrich feather curls gracefully over the tilted brim.

The picture ha of this or various other descriptions is exceudingly fashionable owing I fancy, to its adaptability to all torts and kinds of faces ; for the brim of this variety of hat is generally E 0 constructed as to be bent and coaxed into just the curves to suit each in- dividual wearer.

Hats there are on every side to be encountered in every imaginable style.; and the flat hat or toque seems it anything the mot popular. These generally have a crown of velvet, say white with a brim of -sable or some similarly becoming fur.

Occw•ionally, a enlist looking upstanding aigrette gives point to the whole chapeau ; or a twist of softly tinted good lace forms a soft twist on the crown and falls over the hair at the back. Other hats of a plainer order have a crown of Dongh felt with a brim of folded velvet of a deeper or contrasting tone. Bright emerald green and white is a contrast very fashionable especially Pi nco the combina- tion of blue and green beeline too general to be worn by the beet dressed wontlen. The pretty evening blouse illustrated is made of soft pink silk with a collar and fall of lace from the elbows. Two soft full bows of soft
Oat, A , to, /I"; /47'4 h A SMART COSTUME.

div.head: 'RETTY BLOUSE.
div.p: 'RETTY BLOUSE.

creamy chiffon are arranged in front at eit:ier side in an original and chic fashion. This blouse could he worn with either a pink or a cream silk shirt. Even in old black silk blouse would look very smart with the lace arranged on neck and sleeves in this fashion and some soft cream chiffon bows at the front. It is wonderful how a few tasteful decorative touches will work wonders with an old gown and enable it to do duty for home evening., if for nothing more important. I saw a very pretty idea expressed most successfully by which the blemishes of an undoubtedly parss4 blouse wcrc cleverly con- cealed. g his was brought about by a thin cream lace bolero finished with a flounce of lace at the lower edge and at the elbows.

A liberal amount of very narrow black velvet ribbon was tastefully interthreaded in an effective manner and made still more effective by numerous small cut steel buckles which glistened and sparkled enticingly. COQUETTE.

GAVE HIS CASE AWAY.

" I would say more," wrote a Member of the House I of Commons as he sat in the library there pennmg a letter to • friend, " but that tall rascal, the Memb*r for Bribeboreugh, is looking over my shoulder and reading every wird of this." Whereupon the tall legislator shouted excitedly, "It's false—l haven't !" This is giving away one's case with • vengeance ; yet hardly more so than the people who claim for a particu- lar medicine th.t it will cure certain ailments if the: persons afflicted with them be curable at all, but which , fell to do so, the sufferers finally obtaining relief from another and different medicine. This is of fre- quent occurrence, and of many arch cases here is one, that of Mrs. Edward Morrie, of the " Royal Oak," Llangallen, Denbighshire,who writes thus on the 11th Ju1y,1902 *--"There are times whore I would rather be abort of food than without a bottle of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup in the house. That medicine has been a veritable blessing to me for nearly seven years. I suffered from a very bad form of indigestion, for which I took a certain widely-advertised pill; but it afforcei me no relief at all. The pain and fullness at the ctest after eating seem, dto weigh me down, while if a knife bad been inserted betwE en my shoulder-blades I don't think I could have suffered more. The pain came nre about half an hour after meals, and as it !ncreasf d in severity its effect upon my general health was very bad My stet p aa, much broken at night,and in the morning I had usually such a bad taste in the mouth that it quite destroyed any appetite I might have had for break. fast. Soon I began to dread mealtimes, fer I knew too well what punishment they meant for me,and I went about my housework like one half-dead, thin, pale, and looking miserable. D zziness and a stuffed, bloated feeling, were other symptoms I am not likely soon to forget. At times everything seemed to swim around me, while my eyesight would bt-comP quite blurred. Then th.et bleated or swollen teeing ! was so pronounced at times that it was quite a relief to loosen my clothes. Per three months I suffered like this, and I should have broken down entir, lc but for Mo her Seigel'a Curative Syrup.. That went directly to the root of the in, and by the time I had taken toe firs: bottle I was much better and stronger. If ever there was a sign of the old sympt ma, Mother Seigel'a Cura- tive Syrup never tails me—hence ;my pleasure in giving this testimonial frr publication. It is impossible to praise it too highly."

div.head: RECORD SChOOL ATTENDANCE AT EARLESTOWN. --- Presentation to Three Scholars.
div.p: RECORD SChOOL ATTENDANCE AT EARLESTOWN. --- Presentation to Three Scholars.

There was an interesting ceremony ati the close of the monthly meeting ef the Neveton-in-Makerlield Urban District Council, held in the Town Hall. Earlestown, on Monday evening. The Chairman (Mr Ormand) had the pleasing duty devolved upon him of presenting gifts to three school children who had made record attendance. at school. The three fortunate recipients were AIM Saekey (who had been neither late pot absent from school tor le years), Mary Foley (who had bpen absent only l days in 10 years) and Percy Fitzgerald (who had been absent only ne day in nine years.) The children were accompanied by their parents. The Chairman remarked thaelv had been a member of the School At, en iance Committee for %early 13 years but that was the first occasien on which they had had the pleasure, be thought he might say the honour of re- ceiving the parents of eche ol chileren to be commended rather than taken to task for their iedifference in regard to their children's name-teemy at school. When the question of introducing compulsory attendance a. school was mentioned in the House of Commous some 32 years ago during the di cession of the Educatiou Bill of 1870 it was said that Engiiiihmen would not submit to it, that it would be irnpneeible to ente rce it, and that failure wculd he the only result. He was very thankful to say that ill those prophecies bad turned out to b wrong. Compulsery attendance at tchool bad been a very great ewe 88. (Hear, her.) He could not help but rofer to the discretion and efficiency with which the various authorities had exercised their powers and thev had also been readily eupplemented by the heeds, and wiling co-operation of the parents of the children. (Hear, bear.) There wire, unhappily, and be was afraid would continue to be, parerits who were so utterly in- different to their children's future welfare that the law had to be enforced from time to time against them, but if they took the whole of the statisic- they would find the percentage was vers small indeed. That was neither the two, nor the opportunity to refer to these imp:imitate phases of educational work. They had that day to m-irk an epoch in the hi,tory of the School Attendance Corn• mittee of the Newton-in-fdakerS Id district,but whether it was to be written in the last chapter or w`iether it would mark a new era or not was for the Eiucation Bill now before Parliament to determine for them. Tb three children before him had been very fortunale. `They must have been blessed with good health to enable them to attend school reeulailv and pucctually for 8 many years, and if there was anything to be that:kW, for more thar another,it was for that vi ry great filessing. There were other children who would have been in a similar position bias unfortunaiely circumstances over which they had bad no control. bad prevented them from being in tbe honoured position in wiiich the three children before Lim occupied that clay. They Could not help their eympthies going cut to these children who bad made these record atteneances The pareet, were also to be congratulated because their children by regular and punctual tete dance bad acquired a habit which WCltild stand them in good area I when they wire called upon to earn their livelihood and to take an intelligent interest and share of rrsponsibilit in tire well-being and good government of the village, town or &sr in which they might live. Be was afraid that in the formation of character they were too prone to forget the important part that schoolmasters awl echoolmistreeses played, (Hear. hear. They in the Newton district were exceptionally fortunate in baying beadmaate's and hi admistresses—ard his mama:a alio applied to the staff—of their public schools,who poßsesse sterling it tee/it's , sob, lily attanurrf nts and high rrer,l worth. When they had these vital trit cils uncon- sciouely set before the children day by n•iy and week by week, their ii fiuence must be very great dpon them, (Bear, bear). When the committee knew that ',tact] attendances had been made by these ter - cleildren, the members felt that a suitable gift ought to be made to each child to mark tie committee's arprecia- tion of their regular and puuctull attendance. He had now much pleasure in presenting the gifts on behalf of the committee. (Appbusr).

The Chairman Men presented Alice Sar.ky with a handsome work-bcx and writing ef4k ; Mary Fole‘ with a beautqul aod compact lad's companion ; and Percy 17,!zgeral1 ith a choice writing detk. Mr Gitmour added a few wade. and the father of each child acknowledged the gift of the committee in tuitat le terms.

div.head: EXAMINER FRID N DECEMBER 5 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRID N DECEMBER 5 1902

Well, mates, you are sattinta, r nape r says Jack, quietly. "Thoroughly, Boss. You have carried out the contract like a man. We may now leave old Sydney for a spell, but won't there be a blooming racket on Monday morning." "I expect there will be, but you'll be out of it, and I can cover my tracks. Mates, I have been good pal to you, have I not ?" "The best going." "Then do me a favour; take this drunken sot, the professor, with you and land him somewhere, for it won't do to leave him here."

"You are right, mate, he might split on us," said Barney. "We'll land him in America, where he is sure to prosper in that business of his." "That will do, Barney; take him with you, and here, give him this five hundred quids; we couldn't have done without him, and its only right we should look after a chum."

"Particularly if he is dangerous, as this one happens to be. Here, boys, hoist the carcase along with the property." They raised the intoxicated and drugged psycho- metrist and dragged him off to the cabs at the corner along with the loot, while Jack watched them going, with an abstracted air. Half-an-hour afterwards the psychometric establishment was minus servants, attendants, and professor; then Jack turned with a heavy sigh and led the pony with the dog-cart into the street.

He locked up the back-yard gate and no one 3hecked his course as he went along. The police- man at the corner touched his hat to him when he passed by. He thought nothing of the eccentric movements of the white-haired partner of the fashionable fortune-teller, for he had become used to his ways. Often had that pony taken an early morning exercise during the past week. As Jack drove along he looked at the stars and tried to console himself with the reflection that no 3ne could foretell what might happen in a cam- paign. Warriors go out to battle and kill for their country, and no one thinks of blaming !hem.

A life had been taken that night accidentally. On Monday morning there would be a wild excitement and a big reward for the murderer, but he would be with his faithful and loving Rosa then, with all his tracks covered and an assured future before hirn—that surely was worth the candle he had burnt, the risks he had run.

Four o'clock, and he is at Mr. Chester's house, the bachelor establishment which this astute lawyer keeps. Jack Milton knows very well that the housekeeper has a holiday this morning, there- fore he is safe, so he leads his horse and trap inside the back gate, and when he has shut that he knocks at the kitchen door softly. A moment, and then the door opens gently and a voice asks-- "Who is there?" "Jack, with some baggage." "Bring it inside." Mr. Chester does not help the housebreaker with his burdens, and the packages are lifted from the dog-cart and carried indoors in the dark. Then, when the door is closed and fastened, Mr. Chester strikes a light and looks at his visitor with a scrutinizing gaze. "What is this you have brought in these bags? "Fifty thousand pounds in gold," replies Jack Milton, quietly. "Put them away for me and invest them."

"All right, leave them there for the present." "Have you told Rosa I'll be home to-night?" " Yes ; she expects you." replied the lawyer. " Good, I'll go now. "Good morning." "Good morning." They part with these words, and Jack leads his pony and empty dog-cart out of the gate, which the lawyer closcs and bars after him. Then the housebreaker drives away into the open country at a furious pace.
CHAPTER V.
THE END.
They had a small tea party at Trumpet Tree Cottage on the Sunday night when Jack Milton came tack after his two years' absence. . , .

It is right and propel. for a man to apprise his wife and friends of his home-coining, whether he has been absent for a short or long period—particu• larly it for a long period. Surprise, aro 41,'imi Tilfiti,ant either to the receiver or the one who gives them. Nome men in Jack's position might have felt inclined to play the romantic and time-honoured joke of entering the cottage suddenly and disguised in rags, just to see how darling Rosa and her parents would receive him. Jack could hardly do this, even if he had been disposed, since he had entrusted a considerable sum of money with Rosa's cousin before he went away. He was not disposed, however, to this sort of romance. He had always liked to pose as a rich man, he liked also to be entertained and made much of by his friends, and did not care how much he spent to gain this end. He loved his wife Rosa with all the reasonless intensity of his lawless nature, and to have doubted her so far as to have tested her truth was beyond his strength. She had said she loved him, and she had married him, which seemed proof sufficient for his vanity and his desires. She seemed delighted with his presence, therefore, like a good husband, he took it for granted that she mourned his absence as good wives ought to do. The lamps were lighted and all the stars were out when he drove up to the front gate, not this time in the dog-cart or with his white wig on, but in a cab, with portmanteau and bags beside him, as if he had just come from a journey. Rosa was on the look-out for his arrival, and ran eagerly from the verandah up the little walk to the gate, and here she flung herself into his arms, regardless of the grinning driver. "At List, you old darling Jack." "A', last, my fairy," replied her husband, fondly, as he clasped her to his heart, and then they went indoors like two lovers. Rosa Milton lived with her father and mother, or it would be m^re correct to say, since it was Jack's money which had furnished and kept up the house, that the parents of Rosa lived with her.

The sire of Rosa was a genial, old, and gentle- manly loafer for all that, and looked quite a reapectable father as he sat in his arm-chair, with the Sunday papers before him, his spectacles on his well-shaped nose, and his silver grey beard floating over his black vest. Mrs. Muligan, his good lady, bore out the appearance of a highly respectable matron as she sat eside the teapot and dishes ; and altogether there was a decided air of home-like comfort about the lamp-lighted and well- furnished front parlour. Rosa was like the generality of her Sydney sisters, creamy conplexioned, with features almost classic in their regularity, strongly defined eye- brows and clear grey-blue eyes with a plentiful supply of golden-brown hair. She appeared small beside her tall husband, yet she was above the average height of women, and possessed a figure which for symmetry would have won the approval of the most exacting lover of the beauti- ful. Clearly the road to Jack's heart had been by the eye. They were a magnificent couple, and most people would have agreed that they were well matched. Jack with his strong, dark face, square jaw and powerful frame, and Rosa with the seductive wiles and graces of a Helen. A disciple of Lavater might have found characteristics in both these attractive faces to make him pause and wonder; as, indeed, he could have done in the other face. here gathered round this festive board, Mr. and Mrs. Muligan and Mr. Arthur Chester ; but Cupid'. glamour had blinded Jack, and what the others thought did not interfere with the warmth of their welcome to the new arrival. __

_ The viands were lavish and well enough cooked, for most colonial women are adepts at home work. A couple of fowls, with a ham and a prime joint of beef, flanked by roasted kimer6s, pumpkins mashed, and mounds of tempting tea cake. Mr. Chester carved the fowls and ham, while the gentlemanly father cut the joint, and the mother poured out the tea, thus leaving Tack and Rosa with nothing to do except eat, drink, and look tenderly at each other. After tea was cleared away, at Jack's request Rosa and her cousin went to the piano and sang duets. Jack was fond of singing, though he could not sing himself, and Rosa had a clear, if some- what metallic voice. She did not play, but Arthur Chester managed to accompany her and himself with a creditable "vamp," therefore that part of the evening passed away very well. Then, when the whiskey decanter had been put upon the table and the pipes were lighted, Jack began to tell his adventures of the past two years, in the South Seas, and in this he proved himself a perfect master of fiction. Othello could not have done better, nor could Desdemona have listened with more rapt admiration and devotion than did Rosa as she sat on a low stool at his feet, her pretty tea- gown falling in graceful_folds about her, and her
THE END.

wrlfte arms 15areTO the elbows as the wine weeves dropped back. She rested those white and shapely arms on his strong knee, with her full chin on her ring.covered hands, and those steadfast, clear, blue. grey eyes .faxed on his black eyes. Occasionally, however, she shifted her head slightly to glance with a kind of wonder at her attentive parents, or the quietly observant cousin. When she glanced at Arthur Chester and caught his eye a slight flush crept up and tinted her creamy cheeks, and a tiny curl lifted her upper lip, revealing her white teeth and the redness of her full and moist lower lip. At these times only a gleam shot between the eyes of the two cousins and then she turned her face once more with touching admiration towards the fertile. minded Jack. "I shall call round to-morrow evening after office hours and have a business talk with you, Milton," said the lawyer, as he rose to his feet about nine o'clock and prepared to take his departure. "Do," answered Jack, also getting up. "I intend to spend to-morrow at home and take it easy." "I expect you'll be interested in the newspapers after beimg so long without them." " Yes ; I'll put in my time that way. You get the papers, I suppose, Mr. Muligan ? " " Yes ; the Herald. I'll bring it up to your bedroom," replied his father-in-law. Rosa now proposed, as the night was warm, that they should see her cousin a little way towards his house, and as Mr. and Mrs. Muligan were not inclined for the exercise, the three young people went out together, Rosa in the centre with a hand through the arms next to her of each of her com- panions ; in this fashion they went, linked together.. into the night.

Jack Milton did not venture out of doors the next day, but Rosa, like a dutiful wife, brought him all the newspapers, the Town and Country, the Australasian, and the dailies, to amuse himself with, while she went about her household duties. Rosa liked to work in the kitchen with her mother and the servant, and had some favourite dishes to cook for him, therefore he had to yield and do without more than a flying visit now and again from her, and a fugitive kiss, while he helped his father-in-law to "loaf." _ _

The papers interested both men very greatly, for they were filled with the account of the great robberies which had been discovered on Sunday morning. Jack groaned inwardly as he read about the dead body of the confidential clerk being dis. covered. It was the first man's taking off which could be laid to his charge, and it made him feel uncomfortable, even although he tried to persuade himself that it was an accident. He had, however, great command over his features and feelings, and read the account cuite calmly out to his wife and his father-in-law. Mr. Muligan listened with the interest such a sensation raises in one, while Rosa, with a slight shiver of horror, hurriedly left the room for a moment, and then as quickly returned. •

" I expect there will be a big reward offered for the murderer, Jack," she said, fixing her clear blue. grey eyes on him. "I expect so, little woman," replied Jack, with his glance still on the paper. Mr. Chester came after the lamps were lit, with the evening papers in his pocket. "Have you seen the accounts of that big robbery and murder in George Street?" he asked, as he entered. .
"Yes," replied Jack and Rosa together. "Any more about it ? "

"The bank people have offered a reward of five hundred pounds for information which may lead to the capture of any of the principals," As he spoke he turned for a moment from Jack and cast a straight glance at Rosa, who looked down at the tableoloth and began to smooth it out.

"The police headquarters will receive the infor. volition and pay the reward," continued Mr. Chester. and then they all sat down to the usual hign or dinner tea and began talking about other topics. After tea, Rosa said to her husband-- "I am going out to-night, dear, to see a girl friend in town—Mrs. Gray, you remember? and as Arthur has come to discuss business with you I'll leave you alone for an hour or so. I won't be late, darling. Will you stay till I come back, Arthur?"

"Ni', Rosa, I must be going soon as I have a host of letters to get through to-night." He did not look at her this time, but she looked at him; a lingering look which blended a little con- tempt with some other emotion. " Very well, I shall say good-night. Now I'll leave you gentlemen alone to discuss business. Depend upon me, dear Jack, I'll not be late." She rose and left them with these words, Jack smiling fondly on her as she quitted the room, then the two men sat down squarely to business, for Mr. and Mrs. Milligan had gone early to their own apartment. When the business was gone through Mr. Chester rose to leave. "This is a serious affair, this murder as well to robbery, isn't it, Milton ? " " Ye', very serious, and one to be regretted," replied Jack. "I can depend on your promise made to me, I suppose ? " " Yes, no one shall ever say that Jack Milton did not keep his promise." "Good, and good-Light." After Chester had departed, and until Rosa re- turned, Jack experienced a singular fit of dejection. Everything had gone right with his schemes; the horse and dog-cart were over the cliffs and his wig and spectacles and clothes were destroyed. He had lett no traces that he could think about. His companions were clear away, for they had arranged that beforehand, and yet the spirit of that confi- dential clerk seemed to be haunting him. He went to the sideboard and took as Many whiskeys as he dared take, to brace up his courage and give him some of his lost pluck. He dare not take much drink in case he might talk and get reckless. He looked at his revolver which he found in good order, and then before he got quite too desperate with himself, darling Rosa came back, beautiful and tender.

His wife took him straight away to bed and said she would shut up the place after she had seen him comfortable. She even went the length of going to the kitchen and brewing him a glass of whiskey hot as a night cap, but although he felt he had taken enough, he did not like to refuse the dear girl, therefore he made some excuse to get her out of the room, long enough to enable him to throw the stuff out of the open window, and pretend he had takeN it. _
She laid her creamy soft cheek against his for a moment when she had brought him what he wanted, and gently kissing him on the lips said—
"Now, dearest, let me go and see that all is safe in the house, and then I'll come to bed."
She left him with these loving words, and stole gently down the stairs in her stockings, taking the lamp with her and leaving him in dark- ness.

For a moment he lay thinking fondly about her, and plannin4 out the future; then his acute and trained ears heard sounds outside which banished sleep and woke up his faculties. He stole softly to the open window and peered out, to see forms of men surrounding the house. He knew what that meant to him.

Down the stairs he crept like a phantom, with his revolver in his hand. Whispering voices in the dining parlour lurid him on, and he turned in that direction and listened by the open door. "You must be patient, yet a little while, for he is a strong man. In •a few minutes he must be asleep, for I have giN en him a strong dose of chloral"
This was the voice of his darling Rosa, and another replied----- _

".Ell wait, missus. Hadn't you better go and stay beside him till he drops over?" "Yes . • I'll go and see him now." He did riot wait for the lovely traitoress to come out of the parlour, the revulsion was too great for his wild untrained and passionate nature. With- out a pause he planted the revolver to his brow and Dulled the trigger.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESEELVED./
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESEELVED./
A PROFESSOR OF THE
BLACK ART,
BY HUME NISBET, (Author of" Bail Up," &e.)
PART 111.-CHAPTER IV.
TREASI7RE TROVE.
One o'clock Sunday morning, and four resolute men are assembledin the new establishment, discuss- _ .

leg under-done steaks and strong tea, for they are different from the professor, who lies in a hoggish. state of stupor beneath them. They have work to do to-night that will make or mar them, and they require no wines or spirits to brace their courage, up to the point for daring robbery, or cold blooded murder. They are colonial born and the grandsons of convicts, inured to the sport of hunting- from their earliest years and astute as. savages on the war-path; besides, they would rather gain their livelihood in this way, with its deadly risks, than live by any other means. They cannot help themselves, they are wild beasts, with a coating of craft and cunning, bred from convict fathers and mothers, and gifted with only the one ambition to excel in their guilt. Jack ambition, is the only one amongst them who has no convict antecedents. He had become a

master criminal, as Cromwell became a soldier, through the force of circumstances, but now he dominated them. They wanted fresh blood and a leader, for although they were wicked enough and false enough, yet the creative and inventive genius seemed to be denied. He was a big fellow amongst them; he eould and did plan great coups, and he had, what they could not exactly - interest in his friends; there., his talent in plotting out schemes, -At getting thent out of scrapes, and they instinctively bent to the principle which they could not understand—his good faith. Each man of that small gang would have sold Jack Milton if it had been made worth his while, yet each man knew that he could trust Jack Milton to a penny-weight. It takes a lot of personality to persuade state-school-trained savages to trust in any one. The women were there, the smart handmaids whom Jack had chosen. They were the keenest criminals in Sydney who had managed to escape, for six full days, the supervision of the colonial detectives. The page boy was a young imp who had served hiin on former occasions and who could be trusted as a setter. "Girls," observed Jack when supper was finished, "you know your duty while we work. Cecil, my son, when you see the policeman approach give us the hint—he passes and looks into the open pawnshop every three minutes; six minutes will do our business if all goes well there. The bank is guarded by a watchman, a housekeeper and a confidential clerk ; a dog was there an hour ago, but Barney has silenced him. I'll undertake to quiet the watchman, the housekeeper and the clerk. Do you require any more grub or liquor?" "No, Boss, we have had enough. We are ready." "Come along then, get to your posts, Cecil, and you girls; three quarters of an hour are all I need to do this business in, the biggest in my life." "What about the professor," enquired Barney, looking down on that prostrate hero. " Oh, he is all safe, I dosed his last glass of Burgundy," replied Jack. "Come on boys and brace yourself up for work. The pawnshop first." They all put crape masks on their features, by way of precaution, not that they expected to be seen, yet still it was best to be on the safe side. Silently they foll)wed one another down stairs and into the commodious cellars of the establish. tnent, the professor still sleeping the sleep of Unconscious infancy, while the girls and the page boy crept outside. It was with some pride that Barney showed them the excavations he had made, on the one side, from the cellar to the bank, and on the other from the cellar to the pawnshop. They had the game clear before them if they could escape the watchful gaze of the police on the one aide and the inmates on the other. Jack and Barney were the mechanical engineers of the concern; they had bored the holes, and in a few seconds made the trap door to admit them to the premises of the pawnbroker, then they were all through and in the full glare of the gas-lights and the open windows to whoever passed, for the pawn. ' broker had no shutters. Jack and Barney waited a second and then they rushed forward pulling down and piling up boxes and packages between them and the window. In two minutes exactly, the barricades were raised in a natural fashion and they could lie panting behind, while the policeman made his cursory survey. The next portion of the work was easy as far as detection went, although requiring immense pre- sence of mind and personal strength. Three great safes were standing by the walls filled with valuables and money, but Jack Milton had his plans arranged beforehand ; therefore getting all the clothing and soft pledges he could from the shelves he pitched them on the floor and then, with their crow-bars and levers they over- turned the safes and rolling them one after the other, shot them down into their excavation shafts where they could break them open and examine them at their leisure. It took the four experts nine minutes to remove these iron safes that would have taken expert workmen a couple of hours, such is the effect of sport or excitement on the spirits and muscles of men. The other business was

simple after this exploit, te dart to the till and rifle it between the visits of the police and to take what else was of value, leaving the show cases un- touched in the windows. In fifteen minutes from the time they had entered the pawnbroker's pre- mises, the deed was completed and the pledges were their property. Jack Milton left Barney and the other two men to break open the safes in the cellars while he penetrated the bank. It was not difficult to enter, for he had under- mined the place and silenced the watch•dog. He also knew where the confidential clerk and house- keeper slept and where he was likely to find the watchman.

One of the young men who had acted as a servant went with him and together they stole upon the watchman, who was fortunately nodding by his table in an ante-room • a chloroform saturated handkerchief soon settle him and they proceeded upstairs. Fate had gone well with Jack Milton up to now. The housekeeper was easily managed, for she was asleep when they entered her bedroom, so that she never knew what caused her to sink into a deeper and more peaceful slumber, but with the confiden- tial clerk it was otherwise.
An attack of toot ache had kept him awake that Sunday morning, so that as the burglars entered the room, lie leapt from his bed and con- fronted them with a loud cry. _ _ _

Then it was all over for the confidential clerk, for without a pause Jack rushed upon him and pressing him up against the wall, gave him the garrotter-grip, one fist on the shoulder and the elbow driven with sudden and savage force against the larynx, stuffing his voice and breaking the apple,. With a gurgling sound the poor man sank to the ground and all was over. Jack Milton was a murderer. lie looked at his victim for a second with horror in his eyes, then with a heavy groan he dragged his accomplice away and made towards the loot. It would be time enough to think of his crime afterwards, at present his blood fired up for the sport.

The dying cry of the clerk had not reached the policemen outside, and all the streets were peaceful on this sabbath morning. Only Jack Milton knew that one life had been sacrificed on this raid, and he kept that secret to himself so as not to disturb the unholy glee of his confederates over their winnings. It has been a rich loot, all in all, with the pawn- brokei's pledges, and the bank hoardings; and he may now retire and exist in love and comfort on his lion's share of the proceeds. He is a wealthy man now, with what he has made to-night and what he had before. But that poor confidential clerk's death has to be avenged. It does not take long to win a battle, kill a stag, or break into a bank ; by three o'clock in the morning the confederates had divided their loot, and made all their arrangements to part company. Jack Milton had his share, all in coins and ingots in his dog-cart, ready to drive off, and the others were satisfied with theirs. A boat at the wharf waits to take them off to a ship ready to sail, and a couple of cabs, already arranged for, hang about a side street. They are taking a parting cup and Jack stands amongst them silently, and thinking of that dead clerk, whom the others knew nothing about yet, the clerk who will hang him, if he is not careful,

div.p: The Darbar for the celebration in India of the Coronation -of the King-Emperor will commence on January Ist, 1903, at Delhi. The latter place was chosen in consequence of its' imperial asso- ciations and its central situation. Owing to the limited house and hotel accommodation, the 'Viceroy, leading officials of the Government of India, and native gentry will reside in camps, which will extend for many miles on every side of the city. The various guests will arrive during Christmas week. The latest dltte at which British visitors should arrive will be by the boat that reaches Bombay on the lltith of this, month, when special trains will run to Delhi. The Viceroy will arrive at 11.30 on the morning of Monday, the 29th, and the opening ceremony will commence. A pro- cession of the Viceroy and Ruling Chiefs on elephants, and officials on horseback, will pass through the streets of the city. On December 30th the Viceroy will open, in the afternoon, the Indian Arts Exhibition, which is to be held in the Kudsia Gatdens, outside the Kashmir Gate. The Coronation Dur'ear will be held at noon on January Ist, on the same site as the proclamation of the late Queen-Empress• took place. The cere- mony will consist of reading of the proclamation, the firing of the Royal salute, and playing of the massed bands. In addition to many thaussnds of visitors, there will be nearly 40,000 troops paraded: On the evening of January 2nd, there will be an illumination in the Indian style, and a display of fireworks. On the evening of January 3rd a chapter of the Indian Orders will be held in the Diwan-i-Am, or throne-room of the Great Mogul. On Sunday, January 4th, a State servicet con- ducted by the Metropolitan of India, will be held. On Monday, the sth, there will be a State ball, and on the Bth and 9th, a grand review of British and Indian troops. On Saturday, 10th, the proceedings close with the departure of the Viceroy.

div.head: BIG BEN TO BE ELECTRIFIED.
div.p: BIG BEN TO BE ELECTRIFIED.

The immense exertion of manual labour necessary n the winding of the Houses of Parliament clock, Big Ben, is soon to be a thing of the past. Big Ben is to be electrified. Already experiments have been made in lighting the faces of the clock with the unknown illumi- nant, and it will not be long before power wound works are a reality. The present way of winding the clock amounts to most arduous athletics. Six times every week two men must turn the wheels, and six hours at a stretch. Sixty-six coils of an iron rope have to be pat round the wheels, and every coil entails 132 turns. Moreover, the prelude to this monotonous task is a climb of 360 steps, to say nothing of the descent

THE WORKS OF BIG BEN ON WHICH ELECTRICAL EXPERIMENTS ARE BEING MADE. when the work is done. Some idea of the im- mensity of the clock may be afforded by the fact that in one minute the extremity of each long hand travels over a foot. These long hands are made of the finest steel, they are 15 feet in length, and two men could travel upon thew in safety and with ease. The dials have a width of twenty-two and a half feet. The pendulum is a little short of five yards in height, it weighs 680 pounds, it has a swing of fourteen inches, and it is so delicately adjusted that the addition of one ounce to its bulk involves a time variation of one second per day. THE DEATH OF DR. PARKER. Dr. Parker, who has attained world - wide celebrity by his preaching at the City Temple, has been ill for so long, off and on, that his death at the end of last week occasioned little surprise though great sorrow. Ever since the death of his wife, three years ago, he has been a more or less broken man ; and last April his health began to fail very palpably. Most of the summer he spent at Worthing, and in September he went to Chesham Bois, in Buckinghamshire, to complete his convalescence. Aid^d by his splendid constitution, he iitras so much better at the end of that month that he was allowed by his doctors once more to occupy his ota pulpit, but the strain proved too great, and after one Sunday of work he again broke down; and n ce then his life has gradually ebbed away, and

div.head: LATE DR. PARKER.
div.p: THE LATE DR. PARKER.

After lingering for some weeks he passed peacefully away last Friday afternoon at his Hampstead home. Dr. Parker may have been eccentric and bombastic at times, but he was undoubtedly a great preacher and a strong man. He was one of those who believed in the strenuous life, and, as he quaintly phrased it, his object in life was "to keep the devil busy." In addition to his Sunday services, Dr. Parker for three and thirty years has always made a great feature of his Thursday morning address, to which a considerable number of city men were attracted. Born at Hexham on April 9th, 1830, of humble parents, he soon began to carve out a line for him. self, and, after a spell of work as a schoolmaster, he commenced his career as a preacher as assistant to Dr. John Campbell at the Whitfield Tabernacle, Moorlields. In 1853 he became pastor of an Inde- pendent Chapel at Banbury, going on to Man- chester half a decade later. In 1869 he was called up to London to take head of an historic but dwindling congregation :an

_ lour years later, seizing the opportunity, he sold the valuable site for £50,000 and founded the Oity Temple, which was opened in 1673. Blaze then he has laboured there unremittingly till the time of his death, dying "in harness," as he would have wished. Truly this has been a sad year for Non- conformists—first, Dr. Newman Hall, then Mr. Hugh Price Hughes, and now Dr. Parker. He was a great man; and his little peculiarities can be passed over. Pulpit references to this active Nonconformist were made throughout the country last Sunday. The Rev. Charles H. Kelly, ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference, at the morning service at the City Temple, said Dr. Parker was a pulpit genius. They had never had a successor to Spurgeon, nor would they have a successor to Dr. Parker. He was a many-sided man, but notably a great preacher. He used to look forward to re- tiring from work to the cottage he had in view in the country, where he would have leisure to read, to think, and to pray. But, instead of a cottage, God had given him a palace and heavenly rest.

THE TROUBLE IN SOMALILAND- The disquieting news which continues to come from Somaliland shows how difficult the task is that the Foreign Office has to deal with. Perhaps the most discouraging phase of the whole business is the news that the native levies cannot be relied upon. We are told that instance* of the inter worthlessness of these are multiply- ing. During the march to Bohotle the spearmen in charge of the camels of the maxim detach. ment bolted, and upon arriving in camp here the Somalis at-

A dispatch from Berbera states that he has returned to the British the stores capturiA by him in the fight with Colonel Swayne, accom- panied by a message of defiance. The loss of so competent an officer as Colonel Swayne is sure to be keenly felt. It will be re- membered that he was called home by the Foreign Office to give full particulars of the campaign, and luggest the solution of the difficulty. He was taken ill before his departure, and is too unwell to return. It is hoped, however, that in a short time he will be well enough to resume his duties. With his intimate knowledge of the country and cam- paign he is a soldier that cannot be well spared.
AN• HISTORIC HOUSE.

The famous Red House of Bexley Heath, erected in the early part of the last century by William Morris, is to be offered for sale by auction. William Morris was one of those who sought to instil into the minds of the architects of his day the importance of abandoning the unpicturesque styles of wl7.;.th they had so long been guilty and which we see so much of even to•day. He was a

man of many parts and virtues—a poet, painter, designer, and architect. In fact, until cast into the shade by the more brilliant work of Tennyson, "The Defence of Guinevere and other Poems," by Morris, was an unrivalled work. F. rd Mados Brown, Swinburne, Burne-Jones, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti were all his friends, and month by month the young friends fore- gathered at the Red House' and perfected each detail of beauty, till Rossetti himself declared that A had become "more a poem than a house." The place is now in a wonderful state of pre- servation, and throughout shows the spirit of grace and strength of form but with an utter absence of trivial decoration. When it was built, every article every utensil had to be designed and manufactured specially, to escape the debasing influence of machine production. The Red House is an object of admiration to all who see it. It gives an impression of harmony and grace and restfulness such as no combination of architeotural " features " could have produced.
WILLIAM MORRIS!.B FAMOUS RED HOUSE, BEXLEY. HEATH.'

div.head: SIR MICHAEL FOSTER, M.P. --
div.p: SIR MICHAEL FOSTER, M.P. --

--• ----- Sir Michael Foster, Unionist M.P. for the University of London, has sent his resignation in consequence of his opinion on the Education Bill. The latter he describes as being not only in conflict with his own convictions, but out of harmony with the .pirit of the University of London, and contrary to the views of the majority of his constituents.

Sir Michal Fos- ter is a man of many attain- ments. He is a fellow of the Royal Society, a Doctor of Civil Laws, a Doctor of Science a Doctor of Laws, and has been professor of Physiology in the Cambridge University since 1883. For many years, his "Text Book of Physi- ology " has been universally WHO HAS RESIGNED HIS SEAT adopted in our AS M.P. nit LONDON UNIVERSITY. great medical schools. He was born at Huntingdon on March Bth, 1836, the son of Michael Foster, F.R.C.S., and was educated at the grammar school of his native town and then at University School and College, London. From 1860 to 1846 he practised at Huntingdon, but shortly afterwards became professor of physiology at University College. A year in this capacity, and he was appointed prmlector of physiology at Trinity College, Cambridge. He was president of the British Association in 1899, and in February of 3900 defeated Dr. Collins, of the L.C.-C., in contesting, the seat he has so quickly thought etteto mut%

MANCHESTER CHILDREN.
Their Seaside Camp at Southport.

A striking feature about Southport last summer was the camp, which provided accommedation erg week for two hundred children from Manchester. A longing for the sea seems born in every Lancashire child, yet a well-known Manchester journalist recently discovered a oring girt who is inclined to rate one pleasure she ex- perienced even higher than the delights of sunny South- pert. This discerning young lady is Miss Mary E'len Bagueley. She lives with her parents at No. 29, Gloucester-street, Giurch-lane, Gorton, Manchester. The reporter gives her store in her own simple words

(From a plate. , _webers, Manchester.) " I was very ill," said Miss Segueley. "It was not only the pains which remained after I got over an attack of rheumatic fever that troobled ins, but I was unhappy and weak and miserable. I didn't get any better until I began to take Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people, although I went to Southport for to. years' running. The first time I came back a lot worse. Tho fortnight I was there seemed to do me no good, and the pains ia say joists seemed to get worse whilst I was away from home. The second year I came back a great deal better, but then I was taking Dr William's pink pills. The reporter learned from Mrs Segueley, the mother, that the girl bad been in a terribly weak state all the fourtesn years of her life. She had been constantly, under the doctor, and about two ye.lra ago had a very severe attack ef rheumatic fever. "When she recovered from that," said her mother " her heart was weak —she suffered from attacks of dizziness and sickness, and these would last a long time. In addition to the ahock- ing pains in her joints she was so sickly and weak that I was really afraid she was in a consumption." "Did that prove to be the case ?" "Well, I would rather she did not know that, so you may guess. After what the doctor told me, about eighteen months age, we sent her away. Silo came back worse. In July of this year we sent her to Southport again. But befere she went, I decided to try Dr Williams' pink pills. She took one box whilst away,and came back bright and fresh and healthier-lookiag. Since then she has taken two more boxes." " I saw the young girl, and she looked well." writes the reporter, and when I asked her which she liked best, Southport or the pills, she smiled and answered,"Well, the pills did me most good,and oh, I was so glad to feel well."

Donglas.Lally,and Peacock combined well, and the latter made several good runs along the touch-line, but Sintoa and Mosby were ever on the alert. The Bradford forwards rushed away with the leather in front of them' and a try seemed certain, but Pea- cock saved. After this Widnes returned to the attack. and Hughes and Peacock both made good efforts to set in. Brear made a very pretty opening, and passed to Carrot. and the latter beat several of his opponents, but was collared by Rispan a few yards from the line. Just before half time Hughes made FL bad kick, and Mosby marked close In. He attempted to place a goal, but failed. At half-time neither side had scored. On resuming Widnes played with great dash.and the Brad- ford defence was sorely tried. They were equal to the occasion however, and gradually worked their way to the centre. Mosby got away, acd passed to Sinton, and the latter looked like scoring, but he kicked over the line. Widnes returned to the attack, and passing by Lally, Down, Rispan, and Peacock ended in the latter scoring at the corner. Tilley failed at the place kick The Chemioals now played up In much better form. and on several occasions ft try seemed likely, but their efforts were successfully frustrated by Mosby b end Surman. Just before the whistle blew the Bra iford forwards came away with a rush, and Tilley had only just time to gather the bsll and kick into touch. Result : Widnes I try (3 points), Bra/ford nil. div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

i" HANGING ON" TO A TRAMCAR.—FINE INFLICTED IT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Police Court On Monday, H ii Burnage. Black Bear House, was summoned for hanging on to one of the Corporation tramcars, during the journey from Rylands- street to Latchford on November 20th. The defendant admitted the offence, but said he did not Know there Was a bylaw prohibiting It.—Mr Stanley Wilson.dePuty town clerk, who prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation, stated that the defendant was engaged In the office of the surveyor to the Warrington Rural District I Council and had rooms at Latchford. For some weeks past the ear conductors had been annoyed by certain cyclists, who rode free-wheel cycles, and WOO caught hold of the oars and free-wheeled alongside them. The defen-la, t wnuld probably net have been prosecuted if that was his first offence He had been repeatedly warned against sects con- duct by Inspector Healey, but without effect. On the day named the 540 car let Rylands-street for LatChford and at Bridge•foot the defendant was seen by the conductor to get I hold of the car and hang on behind The conductor told the defendant about it but he took no notice. Shortly afterwards he told defendant that, a passenger in the car hod eslled his attention to the matter, to which he replied : " If he has , anything to say refer him to me and I will talk to him." He continued to hang on until he got to his lodgings. The penaltyt for the offence was 40s, and ha hoped the Bench would see their way to assist the Corporation in putting a top to the practice, which was not only objectionable but dangerous. The defendant had been known to ride between two cars will' they were passing each other —Defendant said he thought the handle bars of his machine made it impossible to pass between two cars.—The Chairman said the practice was a dangerous one, and it was very necessary that an example should be made in order to give a warning to others. The defendant would be fined 103.

AN ExpuNervE Tnim RIDE. At Mondays Police Court, James Jackson, a stonemason, residing in Heath-road, Penketb, was summoned for refus- ing to pay his fare when riding on a tramcar. and also for assaulting conductor Joseph Clarke.—Mr 9 Wilson. deputy town clerk, stated that on tunday, November 23rd, the defendant was a passenger on the six o'clock car from Rylands-street to Latchford. The conductor (Spencer) collected the other fares, but the defendant refused to pay, and used bad language. Inspector Carter, who came on the car, also asked the defendant for his fare and he again used disgusting language. The Inspector then asked him to leave, but he refused. At Latchford the defendant did not leave the car, and was brought back to Rylands-street, where the assistance of the police was obtained. The defendant, who had had some drink, gave them considerable trouble,lnd had to be taken to the Police Station. There seemed to be an Idea, amongst a certain class of people, that they could conduct themselves on the cars just as they pleased, and it should be put a stop to.—Conductor Clarke supported this statement, and said the defendant struck him twice In the chest, and knocked the other conductor under the car steps. —lnspector Carter corroberated.—Defendant was fined 10s and costs. Defendant.who seemed to look upon the proceed- ing as a joke,said Well, all that for the sake of a penny. I had a good penny rile, though."

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. I.BY A CORRESPONDENT].
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. I.BY A CORRESPONDENT].

The Thel wall nuisance has, for the time being, so far as the Rural Council are concerned, sunk into oblivion. At tti6 last Council meeting the Clerk intimated that Mr • Naylor had again written a letter which was practically a restatement of the case against the Council. Whereupon the vice- chairman effectually closured any possible discus- sion by announcing that as the Councy Council had the matter in hand the Rural Council could not and would not do anything further until the higher authority had pronounced its verdict. Presumably Mr Naylors letter, like many other literary produc- tions, has, accordingly, ere this, found its way to the waste paper basket.

It is satiefactory to note that the Council by a large majority resolved to furnish the Council's medical officials with a gratis supply of anti-toxin for innoculation purposes against diphtheria. The melioal officer pointed out that the anti-toxin treatment for diphtheria was practically universal and was an almost safe preventive.

The County Council are -making a determined effort to resist the decision of the Commissioners respecting the Warrington and Northwich Light Railways. The Rural Council have thrown in their lot with the County authority and the resistance is expected to meet with success.
The chief business at the meeting of the Guar- dians was the voting of the usual Christmas fare to the inmates whic‘l,pleasiug to say, does not include alcoholtc stimulants.

The Wesleyan body in Runcorn have recently been ascertaining the number of pledged abstainers in their ranks. The result is rather an astounding one. In spite of the splenetic outbreaks against all and sundry individuals and bodies, the figures unquestionably prove that Runcorn W etleysns, after ail, are bath " temperate " and " moderate."

THE LATE DR. PARKER. A Tribute from the Rev. John Yonge.

The Rev John Yonge, writing in this month's Wycliffe Church Record " says " : It can be no disparagement of any of the Leaders whom Congregationalists delight to hold in supreme honour to say that, in many conspicuous and distin guishing respects,the loss our denomination sustains in- I the death of Dr. Parker is great beyond words. It is even one of those losses which men speak of as " irre-

parab e." Who, among any of the men we possess, can ever fill the exact place or exert the same characteristic power ? By reason of his commanding genius, striking originality, lofty eloquence, and inimitable power, Dr. Parker has attained and held unriva'led prominence in the foremost ranks of Nonconformity. Since, at any rate the days of Charles Haddon Spurgeon in this country, and Mr. Henry Ward Beecher in America, Joseph Parker has had no rival as a preacher of the Gospel of the Cross. This has undoubtedly been an age of distinguished preachers. Our own churches have been proud of Thomas Binney, Enoch Mellor, James Parsons, Alexander Raleigh, Robert W Dale, Samuel Martin, Henry Allen, Baldwin Brown, and many more. Other denominations have rejoiced in men like Morley Punshon, Hugh Stowell Brown, James Martineau, and Hugh Price Hughes, who has p ssed to his rest but ten days before our own distinguished leader The fame of these men has been national and even cosmopolitan. But, save and except Charles Haddon Spurgeon, no name has been so unquestionably supreme as that of

Joseph Parker. The City Temple, which was built and opened under the inspiration of his miuistry,has been the place which has gathered within its walls "all sorts and conditions of men" from every part of the Kingdoin and every quarter of the world. I well remember on one occasion hearing Dr. Parker say, when announcing the collec- tion in his church, that the seatholders of the City Temple were to be found all over the globe. " We have seatholders in Europe, Asia, Africa and America : in Japan, and in the Islands of the sea They do not often attend ! But they have here their allotted seats to show their interest in our work and to share in its sup- port." This may sound extravagant and eccentric, but nevertheless it was a tribute to the truth which no ether preacher of the age could so accurately have ren- dered. Ministers of every Church and Creed, Anglicans of every school and rank, Roman Catholics, Artists, Actors, Novelists, Scientists, Lawyers,Posts and States- men have found their way to the City Temple, and the Thursday morning Service which Dr Parker established and maintained for upwards of thirty years has corn. manded an assemblage such as no other church has collected in any city in the world. Pre-eminently Dr.' Parker has been a man of the " One Book." He has proved himself "Mighty in the Scriptures " His great series of volumes of " The People's Bible," and latterly his striking achievement of " The Pulpit Bible," are powerful evidences of his mastery of the Holy Book, of his veneration for its teaching, and his conviction that the Christian preacher has no need to become expositor of Shakespeare, or Milton, or Tenny- son or Browning while the Bible remains. His own preaching was exclusively Biblical. He broke the bread of life in every sermon he preached. He ever had his own distinctive way of stating and illustrating the truth, but none who knew him and were familiar with his ministry can question his unfaltering fidelity to the Gospel, the Cross, and the Christ. If possible, his advancing years witnessed the growing enthusiasm of his proclamation of Evangelical Truth. He ruled his audience from his pulpit with a sceptre that never failed. He could melt them to tears by the tender pathos of his sympathy, or rouse them to passionate enthusiasm by the vehemence ef his appeal. He could awaken the irresistible smile, even the irrepressible laugh, of the humour which gleamed and sparkled and played in speech and look and gesture. He knew how to drive home his points as " nails fastened in a sure place," and but few of his listeners ever came empty away. Dr. Parker, great and distinguished and commanding as were his talents and his character, had his foibles which sometimes irritated and even annoyed his admirers and friends. They were the defects of his tness. His brethren sometimes failed to understand anct hesitated at seme points to follow his lead They have been known sometimes to "wonaer what Parker would say or do next !" Occasionally the criticisms which gathered round him made one fancy that there was in them the yellow tinge of jealousy and envy of a genius that none could emulate I Dr Parker was not easily harmonized with denominational customs, or speedily taught to repeat ecclesiastical shibboleths. He ever dared to speak his mind, and sometimes in terms that were blunt and uncompromising. Yet notwith- standing these features which laid rim open to criticism and even censure, he was a man whom to know was to love. He was big brother to his smaller brethren. The poor had in him a helper. He was simple, tender, true, artless as a child to any who yielded him confidence and affection. The only occasion when Dr Parker visited "Wycliffe " was on Friday evening August 8, 1890, when he was on his way from Llandrindod, Wales, to visit Cavendish Chapel Manchester, the scene of his Lancashire Pastorate. It had been not a little difficult to secure him, but he himself declared that the "per- sistence " of the Pastor had been too strong for him ! It was a notable visit. "Had your minister and I been appointed a sub-committee to discern the worst week in the year, and the worst evening in that week, we could not have found anything worse than August Bank Holiday week, and the Friday evening therein ! " The Doctor preached a memorable sermon from Heb. xii. 1. One of the last occasions when the present writer had any talk with Dr. Parker was towards the end of last year, near the time when the Church had made such gracious acknowledgment in a beautiful address of the 25th Anniversary of the Pastorate. He was much in- terested in the event, and a copy was subsequently sent him of the Pastoral letter in which the congregations goodness and affection were acknowledged. Dr Parker responded in the following characteristic letter which will be interesting, probably to our Wycliffe people. Hampstead, Nov. 22nd, 1901. Dear Yonge,—l have read your Pastoral letter with much interest and satisfaction, particularly the part of it which refers to your wife. It is to me very touching and goes deep down into my heart. It is so true ! You must have had a very gratifying pastorate in that grimy old town of yours! What a hateful place it is, viewed externally and uon-congregationally ! Yet even there Mrs Yonge and yourself have found flowers and music and love ! Pastorates like yours illustrate the best side of Congregationalism ! lam ever, sincerely yours. JOSEPH PARKER. ' We can forgive the caricature of our "good old town" for the sake of the other sentiments of this letter which reflect as happily on the people as upon the Pastor and his wife. The tender allusion to that part of the " Pastoral " which "goes 'down deep into my heart " indicates how keenly sensitive he was concerning his own most desolating bereavement. He never really rallied from that blow. He and his wife were one in a bond which could not long be broken, and which now, surely, is re-cemented in the Deathless Home ! The Church Universal on earth is now the lamenting loser of a Personality, a Presence, and a Teacher that multitudes have learned to admire and love. They thank God for the inspiration Be has sent them through His servant, and pray that, as of yore, so now when He buries His workmen, He will raise up others to carry on His work

35, Hulme-street, Dalton Bank, Warrington. Mr. Mellor, Dear Sir.—Allow me to tender my Sincere thanks to you for the great benefit I received whilst under your treatment with my eyes. I was recommended to you by a little bay at the station. He saw my eyes in bandages, and out of pure sympathy and a knowledge of what you had done br others, mentionel your name to rue. I came and after three (3) visits, was able to see again. You are at liberty to do with this as you think proper.—Yours truly. THOMAS FRANGLETON. A WARRINGTON CASE DISCHARGED INCURABLE FROM THE EYE HOSPITAL.

20, Leonard Street, Warrington. March sth. 1897. Mr Mellor, Dear Sir.—l write to thank you for the marvellous cure you have made of my eyesight. Previous to being recommended to you I had been a patient to the Manchester eye Hospital for over two years, and was discharged incurable. My left eye was completely blind, but after receiving your treatment for about seven mon to., my eyesight Is res.ored, and I can see better than ever. I shall be pleased to recommend your treatment to everybody that needs a cure,— I am, yours sincere (Mat 3. W. SHELDON.

THERE a tone of President Roosevelt's Message. exultation in President ROOSEVELT'S message to Congress. The strenuous Colonel of Roughriders, who gives to the effice of President of the United States an interest such as it has net possessed since the tragic death of LINCOLN, is full of the sense of abounding national prosperity, and of pride at the part w'nich America has of late begun to play in the sphere of world politics. Many of the passages in his message would have greatly astonished the founders of the Republic. What, they might ask, have the United States to do with the policy of the world. How can the holding of the Philippines,—which is said to have vindicated itself more signally than any *policy ever entered into by the Yankees—be reconciled with the prin- ciples on which the American Constitution rests ? And what is the creation of a strong navy likely to bring about except still wider departures than have already been made from that policy of enlightened self-interest, and ,that abstention from interference in other people's affairs, which has made America strong, prosperous, peaceful, and great ?

However, it is those portions of the message which have reference to trusts and tariffs that will be read with most interest and expectation in this country. Those who believe that the limitation or the extinction of great capitalist combinations is an object that should be sought by means of legislation, will probably say that President ROOSEVELT has climbed down. Ha was expected in such qaarters to propose something very threatening. But Mr. PIERPOINT MORGAN will certainly not shake in his shoes as a consequence of the message which was read to Congress on Wednesday: " Our vim is not to do away with corporations, " says the PRESIDENT. " On the con- trary, these big aggrogations are the inevitable development of modern industrialism, and any effort to destroy them would b 3 futile unless ac- cornplished in ways that would pork the utmost mischief to the entire body politic." These ago words of sound, everyday wisdom. If the trusts, or any of them, are to be extinguished, it will be by their own failure, brought about as is most likely, by over-capitalisation. What President ROOSEVELT has realised is that an American Government has no more right to prevent men clubbing their capital together than an Eoglish Government would have had a right to present a response to CORBETT'S appeal when he asked the English people for their twopences, in order to purchase his "Register" when the cost of each copy had been increased by the stamp duty. It is the evil in the trusts that must be dealt with

Says President ROOSEVELT "We draw the line against misconduct, but not against wealth. We wish to favour a man when he does well. Publicity can do no harm to the honest corporation, and we need not be over tender about sparing the dis- honest one." _ _

The reflection inevitably suggested by an obser- vation of this kind is that, in the 'United States, there can be no necessity for new legislation deal jug with dishonesty. Criminal acts are :already provided for, and what President ROOSEVELT says when construed into plain English, is no more than that the law will keep a sharp eye upon such trust corporations as seem liable to early depar- tures from the path of rectitude. The mossage,so far as it relates to those matters,and to tariffs and workmen's unions, is an exceedingly cautious document: rather in the nature of a homily than of a suggested policy of explosive reforms. The PRESIDENT of the :United States is obviously a cautious as well as a strenuous man. His general summing up on the capital and labour question, for instance, as that ' Every employer and wage- worker must be guaranteed the liberty and right to do as he likes with his property and labour so long as he does not infringe the rights of others." This is to plunge into the realm of trvisms, but of sound and well-established truisms. President ROOSEVELT is neither revolutionist nor innovator, in purely domestic affairs, at any rate, though the high imperialist note discernible in some other parts of the message is certainly new in American politics, and is somewhat out of harmony with the theory which unlerlies the American Constitu- tion.

THE spectacle presented The Lords and the by the House of Lords on Education Bill. Wednesday night was almost as whimsical as that which suggested itself to the lively but grotesque imagination of Theseus CARLYLE. There was no naked DUKE of WINDLE. STRAW addressing himself to a large body of peers in a similar state of destitution. The noble lords who eat up to wait for the Education Bill were clothed and in their right mind ; but there were so few of them, and the hour was so much out of the common, and it is so eccentric a sort of thing for members of the House of Lords to sit up at night in their own Chamber because there is a formal duty to be attended to that the whole inzident seems to belong to the region of fairy tale. The whole course of public business at present tends to produce a sense of the unreality of things. The House of Commons has been engaged for some weeks past—at a time of year at which its members usually scatter them- selves abroad or shoot their pheasants at home— partly in discussing and partly in witneseing the passage by guillotine of a measure which is con- demned by the bulk of the people of the country, which is not believed in by many of its own sup- porters, which is intended to snatch an advantage from the nation for the benefit of the Church; and which finally no Government would have dared to propose if it had not possessed so heavily preponderating majority that it could afford to make light of the defections occasioned by the gross and staring injustice of its proposals. It seems hardly credible that such things should be done in such a way. We have been accustomed to regard our two-party system as a means of arriving at equitable arrangements; as a piece of political machinery which preserves us from the falsehood of extremes; and we find ourselves plunged almost on a sudden into a condition of things in which one party, proverbially farneus by the way for its lack of wisdom, sets aside as inappropriate to the circumstances all ideas of give-and-take as between the two sides rep- resented in Parliament, all sense of responsi- bility to public opinion, all consideration of what is best for the future of education in England,and makes use of its majority to pass in a violent and summary manner a really 'epoch-making measure which is admitted to be raw and ill-considerect,and which is not heartily approved by—at a probably extravagant estimate—more than 100 members in a House consisting of 670. The legislative pro- posals made under these circumstances are pre- cisely those which the House of Lords makes a parade of sitting up for till after midnight. The Government is eager to do some- thing dastardly in a hurry, and their lordships are their most obedient servants. The theory has recently been revived that the Upper House is a revising and suspensory body. The Lords have of late years set forth the novel and astound- ing claim to be the real interpreters of the will of the people. This is founded on their rejection of the home Rule Bill; but the Home Rule Bill was the measure of a Liberal Government. Certainly I the action of the House of Lords was suspensory in that case ; but its action is never suspensory where the measures of a Conservative Government are concerned, it was one ot, its own members, I LORD JAMES of Hereford, who called it a committee of the Carlton Club. Only a few nights ago the LORD CHANCELLOR was advising the House in the interests of the Education Bill to pursue a course of conduct which he had him- I self denounced as unconstitutional. On Wednes- day SIR WILLIAM AsTsoli, the Education Minister in the House of Commons, left it to the House of Lords to declare what is the meaning of the KENYON-SLANEY amendment. He said; " He admitted that the debates had shown a greatliilifierenee ot opinion as to the meaning of the Keilyon-Slaney sub-,ect on, and that made if emin- ently desirable that when it Was discussed in another plheti sueti alteration should be made as wrociousltddpu its meaning beyond dispute. It was estrable to have4it filially settled in another place." This is novel sonstitutional doctrine, forsooth. But we are living in a topsy-turvy time. Things happen as in a dream becauss,if the truth must be said,the people have been asleep.

Now that there is every probability of the Education Bill becotning law in March next,rate- payers are beginning to reckon what effect it will have on the local irates. In Warrington it is stated that it will Mean at least a three- rate, others seem to think that the increase will he sixpence, whilst some are disposed to estimate the additional burden at not less than niuepence in the pound. Such advances as these will mean a general increase in rents and this increase will fall most heavily on the poor, who whilst professedly enjoying free educa- tion, will be paying for it through the rent collector. The increase will, of course, in different districts vary according to the educational facilities already provided. In Warrington at least the Corporation will have to embark upon a building scheme right at the outset. The Education Department have already submitted a list of their requirements and it is not a light one. Not only are additions asked for at several of the existing schools but new schools are demanded in certain districts. This will severely tax the 'veal exchequer and with rates at 6s 6d in the £, the prospect of an early increase for educational purposes is not very inviting.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
REMOVING SWINE VVITHOUT A LICENCE.

At Kaucoru -Petty Sessions on Monday, 'Lamina Plant, High-street, was summoned for removing swine without having mane a declaration at Ran- corn On November 19th.—Sergearit Bottom said he saw the defendant in High-street with a cart con- taining a pig. He asked him if be had a declara- tion and he said he had not. He said he was taking the pig to be slaughtered, and was not aware that he bad to get a licence.—Sbrgeant Bottom observed that the Order was posted extensively throughout the county, and had been in force two years. It was well known among pig dealers.— Toe Chairman (Mr A It Norman) said the offence was a serious one. Defendant should have made himself acquainted with the bye-law. They were dealing leniently with him by fining him 2s 61 and 88 6d costs.
HA.LTON WESLEY AN METIE ODIST TEMPER NCR
SOCIETY.

On Tuesday evening Mr Harry Barker, F I C, of Runcorn, lectured on" Drinks and Drinking, by a Deutscher:"The lecture was a criticism of some articles in a German work. The manufacture of spirits was described, also the action of alcohol on the human body. Mention was made of the high price paid for making strong drink compared with the high price paid when used for ordinary manu- facturing purpose. The positions of Germany and England on the drink question were contrasted, much to the former's disadvantage. The lecture was illustrated by experiments with different kinds of alcohol. Rev W T Coppiu presided, and there was a large and appreciative audience. Messrs A Rowe (sec) and W Looker also spoke, and the fol- lowing musical items were well rendered: Quartette "Missing creasurers " Mrs W Hankey, Mrs F Han- key, Messrs E Hankey and A Saunders; dust "Jesu lover of my soul" Misses Ryalls and Goulden ; duet "Albion" Messrs J Norbury and C P Bradbury. Mr R Sutton accompanied.
