div.head: HOIPITAL lIIIESTION.
div.p: A HOIPITAL lIIIESTION.

A letter was ree—eivaliio—m idessrs Dunlop. Wallis, and Ca, solicitors to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, stating that the Company had agreed to the suggestion that the hospital proper should be considered as the property of the Canal Company, and that the (tart shed and disinfecting house should be looked upon as the property of the Council and be removable by than whenever the tenancy might be determined. The Com- pany would be glad if the Council would new alter the agreement in this respect. In reference to this matter the chief engineer to the Manchester Ship Canal Company wrote stating that, considering the length of time which the road known as Lapwing-lane had existed in its present condition, he was unable to see why the Canal Company should be asked to fence the approaches to the bridge now. But he had brought the matter before the directors, who agreed that the fencing should be carried out at the cost of the Company, as far as the approaches to the bridge over the Runcorn and Latchford Canal were concerned. Ho had, therefore, instructed the resident engineer to meetthe Council's surveyor and take the matter in hand On the proposition of Messrs Pilling and Roylance it was resolved that the Council's portion be done.

div.head: TEE KINGSLEY POLLUTION SOMME.
div.p: TEE KINGSLEY POLLUTION SOMME.

The Clerk ro the Kingsley Parish Council wrote stating that be had submitted to the Council the District Council's surveyor's estimate for the piping of a portion of the open brook in the parish of Kingsley. The follow- ing refolution was passed " That in the opinion of the Council the estimate submitted is too excessive, and if the brook was periodically cleaned out and the 'nape°. tor saw that property was in a sanitary condition and sewage dealt with on the premises the brook would be better as it was than by being covered in." Mr Woodward said the scheme prepared by the sur- veyor was far too elaborate and excessive. He thought the surveyor had misapprehended the intention of the Council. The only part that required doing was a length of sixty yards. A re-examination arid a revision of the estimate would be the proper thing to be carried out at some future time. The brook was much more satis- factory than it bad been for years. He thought the matter might rest in abeyance for some time.

The fao3 was that the land owners and others, so that the extension might be made a real benefit to that part of the town. had given land to the Council. Tne committee thoueht that the wisest thing, considering the amount of trait 3 on the road, was to add the land to the road and make a permanent roadway. Mr Brown : What is the total cost of the read ?

Mr Posnett replied that the total cost would be about £1,950. The contribuions in cash had been about £l5O besides the contributions of land and labour whioh amounted to about £9OO. The £1,950 did not include the land given. The Surveyor said that the total cost to the town would be about 11,500. Mr Imison thought the land owners heel been particu- larly generous. The November quarterly session was held in the United Methodist Free Church St Helens, on Satur- day,November 29th at 3 p.m. Bro Rev I A Lee,DCT, presided, representatives were present from all parts of the district, Earlestown being well repre- sented. The reports of the officers skowed active work had been carried on with the result of a large increase both in adult and juvenile sections, Bro Oliver of Liverpool, foreign correspondent read a long list of news from all parts of the world of members of the Good Templar Order. Sister Duncan reported on the orphanage a good sum being realised from the members. Presentation Gavels from Jerusalem were given by the D.C.T, Bro J A Lee to Bro A Francis and Sister Mrs Woods, both of 1 Earlestown, and one to Bro J Lindon of St Helens, for opening out New branches of the Order at Run- corn, Warrington and Tyldesley. The annual Session is to:be held at the Gordon,Smith Seamen's Lodge Institute Liverpool in February 1903, Votes of condolence were ordered to be sent to the ' relatives of the late Revs Hugh Price Hughes and IDr Parker. The meeting adjourned fur tea, after which the good of the Order was discussed. Thanks were tendered to the St Helens friends for the , rrange ments made for the Session.

The Chairman observed that before proceeding with the ordinary business of the Council it was his painful duty to refer to the very great loss their es:eemed Chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee had sustained in the desth of his wife. At a meeting of the Water Committee the Engineer reported that Messrs Gillespie and Mason, Ltd., were willing to lot the Council have a supply of water, if required, at the rate of 8,000 otiose per hour, and that they would make the necessary connections to the mains and supply water at a price not exceeding sixpence per 1,000 gallons,the Council to be at the expects s of provid- ing and fixing a meter and altering the pipes at the reservoir. It was resplved that the Clerk be instructed to inform Messrs Gillespie and Mason that the committee will be pleased to make arrangements for a supply of such water by them as may be required by the Council from time to time. _ _

Mr Berton, in moving the confirm Oen of the Minutes, stated that owing to an accident at the water works the supply had been deficient. They had endeavoured to rectify this by obtaining from the rail- way company the ordinary supply which they formerly depended upon. They had also made arrangements with Messrs Gillespie and Damon to give them assistance is the event of any further breakdown. The breakdown was due tc the contractor not having provided a pump for pumping water from the well. He trusted the ir- convenience would be remedied by the steps the com- mittee had taken. (Hear, bear!. Mr Gilmour seconded, but said the committee would not carry out his instructions with reference to the giving of notice to the residents when there was a scarcity of supply. div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. -- [By "Ovation

Tbank goodness there's a match at Wilderspool to. ! Players and supporters alike are getting dis- heartened by this frequent absence from home,coupled with disaster on the field. Warrington have not lost at home yet and there is no reason why they should. As a rule they do fairly well away, but just lately things have gone badly, Hull Kingston Rovers and Hunslet inflicting the first two successive defeats of the season. But Warrington were fairly beaten on each occasion, so there is not much room for grumbling.

Last Saturday it was Albert Goldthorpe and Hunslet that gave Warrington their quietus --Goldthorpe prin- cipally. Without the "one and only Albert" the Parksiders would be worse off than Warrington are without Fish,and that is saying a good deal. He seems to be playing better than ever just now, and on Satur- day gave a display that quite demoralised Warrington and was admirably adapted to the capabilities of his team. His kicking was suberb in its length and placing while for headwork he would take some beating. I attribute Hunslet's victory entirely to their skipper, even though they carried most of the scrumn2ages and played a fair game ail round.

It was a pretty big experiment on Warrington's part to play four forwards fresh from the "A " team, but the play of the seniors justified the change, and the new men justified their selection. They brought no extra weight it is true, probably they are lighter men, but they showed themselves .f ull of energy and deter- mination which, against a less powerful pack than I Huaslet's must have had a big effect. As it was,War- ring,ton got the ball a good number of times, especially up to half-time, but not much use was made of it. The whole team is playing below par at present. They do not seem to have rallied since the lengthy and lamented George Dickenson" geet strung up," halves and three- quarters alike showing poor combination. What has come over Burgess and Hockenhall, I don't know, but I hope it is only a cloud of a temporary character. Certainly they seem just no s, qu'te incapable of doing the right thing with the ball when they get it. Perhaps there will be a rejuvenation of the Warrington team for Wigan's benefit. The presence of the old familiar crowd and surroundings often has a stimulating effect.

The game at Hunslet was full of interest, especially for the hom4 crowd,whick yelled itself hoarse,for War- rington seemed to have caught yet another team in its best mood. Up to half time however, the game seemed thoroughly open as far as the ultimate result was concerned, for there had been no score and War- rington had shown form as good as that of their oppon- ents. But on turning round what a change was there ! Hunslet came down on the Warrington ei e with grattle right from the kick off. The forwards swept Warring- ton before them, "Albert " screwed the ball across to the corner where Harris made a mess of things and W Goldthorpe scored a soft sort of try which was nevertheless well worked for. There was no goal strange to say. Two minutes later Goldthorpe got hold again from his fellow-half, ran to the line before giving Whitely a sweet and certain try under the posts, which the.originator of the move easily converted. All this in about six minutes ! Then Warrington had a turn and gat hard lines at the corner, but before they were cleared out Burgess found his way over the line from the midst of a scramble and Fish added two more points. Nine minutes gone and thirteen points scored ! Not bad eh ?—except for Warrington. There was slightly less delirious excitement for a time after this, but Warrington were always defending and being pushed down the slope in a rude sort of way. Things were almost getting dull when the referee gave Hunslet a penalty—which they sadly needed of course—right under the bar and "the one and only &c.,"popped the ball over in the old sweet way. Another spell of give and take, in which Fish was very prominent in taking all he could get, and then Goldthorpe tested Harris with another raking cross-kick, which was smartly fielded by Whitely who took Harris over the line with him, and a goal followed. Prior to this, how- ever, I should mention that fish just as cleverly kicked over to Harris at the other end and with a clear course before him the right winger hesitated so that he was tackled. Harris seemed quite off-colour on Saturday, and I never saw him show less resource and dash. Whitely, on the same wing, always stood over him. There was no more scoring and Hunslet won by tnirteen points to five.
Briefly, Warrington were out-scrummaged, out- kicked and out-generalled on Saturday. Yet I shall expect them to get the points back when ilunslet come here on March 28th.

Among individuals Fish was easily the best of the Warrington backs, though 11-. had to make all his own play. Brooks did very well again, and was always I quick on the ball and on the men who had it. Of passing there was none, hardly, so he received little I practice in that department. Knight played a fair game but missed touch too often in aiming for a good length. The two Goldthorpes, hi Whitely, and Gott, a reliable full back, were the best men on the home side. Forward Hunslet are as powerful as ever, and fre- quently pushed Warrington bodily down the slope by sheer strength.

After all Halifax did not go under at Swinton. They showed a more formidable front than against Salford, and managed to share the points. The Reds themselves accomplished another good performance at Leigh,where the high and mighty Mather Laners were forced to bow the knee, and for once in a way actually admit them- selves beaten. Broughton are still second, while at the other end Brighouse trod the Rovers into the mire, and Warrington's recent conquerors are again astride the bottom rung of the latter.
The League Table up-to date is as follows :—.

For. Agit. P. W. L. D. G. T. P. G. T. P,Ffs. Halifax . l3 10 1 2 13 18 80 8 6 34 22 Broughton 11 Swinton Salford Leigh Runcorn Bra Hord l2 6 4 2 14 17 79 10 12 56 14 Oldham Warrington l3 5 5 3 10 11 63 13 14 68 13 Hull Wigan Balky Hunslet Hudler66,ld l2 3 8 1 5 7 11 11 12 58 7 St Helens Widnes Brighouse Rgs Hull K Rovers l3 3 10 0 411 41 19 23 107 6

There is more than average interest being taken in to-day's match with Wigan, for the colliers are reported to be keen on capturing points from the " wirepullers " The clubs stand together in the Lea ;Lie table and have somewhat similar records,except that Warrington have scored twice as many tries as their opponents of to-day, but have had four more scored agaiost them. A win to- day would mean a lift in the League ladder for Wigan, but Ido not believe they will get that lift. The luxury of a home match is too great for Warrington to waFte it, and the utmost endeavour will be nut forth to give ' the Wiganersl a severe trouncing • Wigan have only scored one try in the last eight matches, and that try won the match against Huddersfield on Saturday. Such a record does not speak well for their " five to four " chance of beating Warrington.

I have a gratifying piece of news this week "Jack" Hallam has at last signed on and figures in the team list for today. After an absence of three months he should obtain a welcome from the crowd. There is no doubt that his presence will add considerable cmfidence to the team. Since the opening of the season Knight has filled the vacancy with an ability and pluck which do him infinite credit Not many men could have come into the team, new to the position, and have given satisfaction for three months. He has the making of a class back and I hope he will persevere in the position.

The full team for to-day is : Tiallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Brooks and Harris, threequarters ; Burgess and Hockenhall, half-backs ; Morrison, Elmondson, Harmer, Meacock, Swift, Nayl ,r, Forster and Jolley, forwards

The "A " t2am at Wigan will be Knight, full back ; Watkins, Fillingham, Edmon s, Bailey, three- quarters ; Duckworth and Hunter, half-backs ; Lunt, Roberts, Cress well, Fairhurst, As Elton, E Warbu rto n, and Coleman, forwards.

div.head: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT VULCAN FOUNDRY.
div.p: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT VULCAN FOUNDRY.

liw At the Warriagton County Court on Thursday, before His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, %X., the further hearing of the claim under the Work- men's Compensation Act was proceeded with in which Henry Andrew, of 31, Manchester-row, Vul- can, Earlestown was the applicant and the Vulcan Foundry Company, the respondents. Mr A Browne represented the applicant,and Mr Brearley, barris- ter, Manchester (instructed by Messrs Cobbett, heeler and Cobbett) the respondents.—Mr Brear- ley said the order of the court on the last occasion was that the applicant should go back to work bnd endeavour to perform the duties he was formerly engaged in. The applicant went back in pursu- ance of that order and had continued at that work up to the present day. tie had done the work satisfactorily and earned rather more ' money than before the accident. Mr Browne re- called the applicant,who stated that he had suffered considerable pain whilst working with his injured hand.—Mr Browne pointed out that the applicant had lost the first joint of the first finger, Inc two first joints oc the second finger and a portion of the third fiager of the left hand and these injuries pre- vented him from lifting and gripping materials with the same facility as formerly—Mr Brearley contended that the applicant was ju4 as good a workman, as he was before the accident, for this work. He had done it for two months and nevet made any complaint about pain.—The applicant contended that he had complained.—Mr Brearley said the firm was quite willing to keep the appli- cent on for an indefinite period at the same work. They had put upon the file of the court that they admitted their liability to pay compensation in case any was due. The applicant had been able to work ever since the memorandum was filed. In April last the firm offered to restart him but he refused to go bazlr and was therefore not entitled to any compensation.—Mr Browne con- tended that the applicant had acted under the advice of the works doctor in not resuming work.—His Honour said ha would not make a substantial award as the applicant was able to continue at work. He would, however, make an order for a penny a week and for the .C 5 its lai compensation claimed, with costs

On Saturday afternoon between one and two o'clock, a young fellow named Thomas Critchley employed as a labourer at the Vulcan Foundry Works was engaged with others breaking scrap iron under the steam hammer when a piece of irod flew out and striking Critchley on the leg, caused a compound fracture of the thigh. Dr Mouncey was sent for, and the man was removed in the Horse Ambulance to Warrington Infirmary, where he is progressing satisfactorily.

div.head: SAD FATALITY TO A BOY AT BARLESTOWN.
div.p: SAD FATALITY TO A BOY AT BARLESTOWN.

Oa Tuesday at noon a boy, four years old, named Samuel Simpson, son of ,Nfilton Simpson, of 11, Derby R3W, Vulcan, Eariestown, met with a shock- ing death at a level crossing on the Railway, near his home. He had been to school, and when be reached home he went on an errand to Bridge farm, having to cross the Railway to do so. On returning from the farm, he had got on to the croFsing when he saw the 12.43 p.m. passenger train. Eirlestown to Warrington coming down the bank at a good spesi. The engine driver was lieunding th's whistle at the time, and he saw the boy on the crossing. He suddenly started to run, and must have fallen across the rail, as when found after the train had passed, his body was lying lengthways in the four-foot, the head being almost severed. The supposition is that the unfortunate lad fell in tryiag to get over the crossing in front of the train, and the life guard bad caught him and flung him clear, but in doing so injured him so severely as to cause his death. 'Ft/431)D1&} AT EMILESTOWN.—DRING—CORLETT.

Ap. interesting wedding took place at Wargrave Church, Harlestown, on Wednesday morning the contracting parties being Mr Samuel Driug, arcei- tect of the firm of °mug and Manchester, Reties- town, and Alice Kate Corlett, seconl daughter of Mr B Corlett, timber merchant of Lazare House, Cross-lane, Earlestown. Much interest was taken in the event and a large number of people congre- gated at the church. The ceremony was performed, by the Rev J C.rson, M.A., rector. The bride wore a charming dress of brown zibeline trimmed with white velvet with raised velvet flowers. Her head' gear was comprised of a white velvet hat witu trimming to match. She carried a magnificent boquet comprised of lilies, rase, chrysairtiemums and hyaciaths, with similar trailings. She wore a handeome gold and diamond pendant, the gift of the bridegroom. Her bridesmaid was her cousin Sites Burchall, of Cnester, and she wore a blue cloth dress trimmed with embroidery, and had a toque of velvet and wings. She also wore a gold brooch presented by the bridegroom. The best man was Mr A J Manchester, partner with Mr Dring. The bride was given away by her father. Mr W il Thompson, brother-in-law of the bride, officiated at the organ. A breakfaQt was given at the house of the bride, and the happy pair after- wards left for Colwyn Bay. where they are to spend their honeymoon. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES [OWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES [OWN.
[BY A CORRASPONDEN T.I FOOTBALL.

Earlestown were na-co-Tt--u-n-f-o-rtunate on Saturday in their encounter with Rochdale Town, on the letter's ground. The game was started late, and only six of the home eleven put in an appearance. Earlostown had a golden oppor- tunity of putting on a few goals,but they neglected to take advantage of it. They certainly swarmed round the Rochdale goal and gave the custodian an anxious time. The condition of things was altered . when the missing six men put in an appearance. and the venue of play was changed for a time, Earlestovvn, however, recovered tNemuelves, and played a much superior game to their opponents, 1 but as usual, they were unable to find the net. IRochdale were more fortunate, or more Skilful, and ' chey succeeded in getting the ball past llobin on i two occasions, the result being Rochdale 2, Rules- town nil.

Before the or 'finery business of the meeting was pro- ceeded with,His Worship the MAYOR said :—I may crave a few minutes, and they shall not be lone, to refer to a select which is in the minds of all of you. When I accepted the mayoralty of vour °nutty boreugh for the second year I was tcld that I was doing. sn at the unani- mous request of the Couscil. and that I mi2ht confident- ly rely upon the same uuaeirnous and crr lial support which I had previously mst with ;if I have forfeited your confidence.if ss your Mayor I may he attacked and censured by members of nay awe Council at a public meeting from a public platform for acting on your Finance Committee in strict accordanee with your own bylaws and resolutions, under the guidanoe anol instruc- tion of the presiding chairman, and under the advice of your Town Clerk as legal adviser, and your Borough Treasurer. I feel that with SUCh s very nnlooke,l fer circnestsance it is incumbent upon me, in your interests, and in the interests of Warrington. which I have a, heart, as well as in my own interests, very seriously and carefully to consider my Positien here. (H.ar, bear.) I a; -Inez, for taking an 'utter time, and we will now proceed with the business of the meeting. THE ALDERMANIC VACANCY. COUNCILLOR SMETHURST EXALTED.

The first business on the agenda was the election of an alc'ermen to supply the vacancy caused by the resigna- tion of Alderman Roberts (Town Hall Ward) Councillor PIERPOINT : Before we proved to the election of Alderman,with your kind perrnission,l should like to put a question to the Town Clerk. The MAYOR : Will it lead to env discussion ? Councillor PIERPOINT : It hag r.fo,ence to the election of alderman. Ahotr; the year 1897, an •greement was signed by all the then members of the Council. Such an asvernent regulated the election of aldermen in accordance with Section 1 of the Rule of Precedence, Standing Order 47. Seeing that 16 of the signatories are no longer members of the Council, is the agresmect to be considered by the 20 wbo are still members ? The Town CLERK : It is a personal mater which each member of the Council must answer himsalf. Councillor PIERPOINT : I may take it that th. agree— ment is not in existence as stated by an alderman of the borough • short time ago? The TOWN CLERK : Oily SO fa. SS each individual member of the Council foals himself' bonnd by it. (Haar, bear.) Counciller PIERPOINT : Then it io of non-affect. (Hear, bear.) The voting was theta proceeded with. The MAYort announced tha" 26 had voted fir Coun- cillor Smethurst and one (Councillor Craik) for Councillor Pisrpoint. Ile had the pleasure of anneuncing that Councillor Smethurst had been elected alderman. (Applause.) The MAYOR (turning re Aldtrrian Rrnsthurst) said : I am pleased to be tbe first to congratulate you upon your accession to the aldermanio diemiw. and I am sure no one will carry tae honour better. (Applause.) ALDERMAN SMETHURST'S RECORD.

-- T' newly elected Alterman then returned thank.. Oa rising to 'peak he was very heartily received and said it was a difficult task for him te return thanks to the gentlemen who had voted for hitn, and especially to tha gentleman who had not voted for him,bectanso he had an opinion of his own and he had a perfect right to it. Councillor Craik and he were good friends, and would cookinue to be good friends. (Hear hear.) He should endeavour to be a loya.l and dutiful alderrnsn during the Mayor's term of cffice, and during the office of every other gentleman who was placed is such a high and proud position during his (Alderman Smethurst's) connection with the Council. Warrington was a growing and prosperous town, and it was nn little task to endeavour to fill the pAitiora of the office of alderman. We was succeeding a geirlernan who had Riled the office honourably, faithfully and justly— (hear, beer)—asd with an ability which could not be xpented from a person like himself (the speaker). The town bad honouvd him by electing him alderman. It was not the first time it had honoured him by electing him to a high position,and be hoped be would conri•oe to retain the respect of the people. (Hear, hear.) He was now bidding farewell to a conltiloeec7 he had represented for 11 years. The first time be wad returned to the Council he had ts fight for his Seat, and it bad always bees his intention to act as honestly and as uprightly as he would in his own businese. He would not spend money extravagantly. but be would sperd it as if it were his own. His constituents had no doubt followed him to a certain extent and be thought he had the right to thank them, and to give them and the Council a etalement which he thought they would agree weuld speak ‘or itself. They knew that the duties of a councillor took up a large amoont of time, and it was net all men who had the time at th• ir di.posal or who could afford to give it. After the town had been I pleased to place honour upon him he felt it was his duty, to give as much of his time as possible, and work to the best of his ability for the town that had honoured him so greatly. He did not think it would he out of place te give them his attendaucee. which would thus go te' his constituents withent his publishing them en the walls. During the last three years he had given no little time to the work, in the fire year he Wended 158 meetings, in the nest- 159, and in tho third 147, making a total of 464. iii had also attended 16 fire engine practices, and he had attended to the police courts din.- may the last three VPM s 293 tisl:l34,rnakine a total .1 773, which made an aware?, for three wars in succession of 257. (Applause.) That was indepeodont of email com- mittees and deputations and other things which took Or .0 and four and rome even five hours Is various wave. He thnugh'i that his constituents would be eatis• fled and that tnev woull los nroud that the Council had so far honoured him as to make him an ra,derman, and he trusted he would fulfil the duties to their meisfac- tion. (Applause.) Alderman SAIETMYR T then made the customary de- claration, and, upon the motion of the MAYOR, er_rooded by the DEPOTY-MAYOR, lie was elected the presiding effizer for the Town Hall ward, in succession to Mr Roberts, -

ALDERMAN FAIRCLOUGH AND PARR HALL CRITICISM. COUNCILLOR DODDS WITHDRAWS NOTHING. LIVELY PASSAGE.

At a meeting of the Finance and Eitate Committee•on the 24th November. it was resolved on the motion of Councillor Dodds that no order for the payment of aecounts have been passed by the respective com- mittees. Tho DEPUTY MAYOR (Al lerman Fairelough) in moving the adoption of the misiutes, said that it was stated at a meeting held in the Pare Hall on Novomber 25:h "that many of the R cccunts which c-trne before the Finance

Committee hai no mark upon them to show that they I had been examined and passed by the committees, I specially appoiated to see that such accounts had been properly authoriz id, that the goods bad bean properly supplied, and at the contract rates, and that in connec- tion with the Town Council orders on the bankers are signed several days before the accoeunte for which the payment was proposed,had been examined and certified by the responsible officer." Another speaker stated "it was not good finance to pay on the Monday and chetile the accounts on the following Friday." The fasts were ' that at the last two meetings of the Finance Committee orders were signei for the payment of accounts nernber- ing See ; of these, 29 only apeesred en the supple- mental isehedu'es. Those schedules were used in accord- ance wito the following resetution of the Council of Bth January, 1901 .—" That is order to avoid delay in the paymnnts on amount of contracts, the But mg* Treasurer be instructed to prepare a supplemental schelule of the amounts certified by the respective eneineers to be passed at the first msetiae„ held after the receipt by the Borough Treasurer of such certificates." The aertificatee of the amounts due to the contractors were in every cage certified by the responsible architeot, enehiteer, or official ; the certificetee ware subsegeently laid before the respective committees, and payment was not made until they had been duls pa3ssd. With re- spect to the SPeCilic meationed at the meeting,that was a payment of £730 te Mr Davenport on amount of a contract for the Technioal School. It was duly certified by Messrs W and S Owen, the architects, and contained a statement of the amouct paid to the date of issue ; the certificate was laid tefora the Museum Committee on the 14'h November, and was not paid until after that Imeeting. Those certifiestes, as was well known, were practically payable on demand. He male this state- ment to show that the Finance Cemnaitteo was only carrying out the instructions of the Couocii. Alderman Motres seconded the adoption of the minutes. Ce incillor Donbe : I arts the person who made the charga in Parr Hall and (w.rmh9) I withdraw nothing." (A.oplause from the public.) There were accounts before us with no mark upon them at all. I arts prepared to show that, and I am also prepared to show that you are acting contrary to your own Stand- ing Orders in submitting accounts to the Finance Com- mittee le.fere they had bees checked and pigged by the committees responsible for the expenditure. I withdraw nothing I have said anywhere with regard to this business. (Applause.) The MLYIR observed that although the Standing Order referred te,wal actually on the book, the resolu- then mentioned by Alderman Fairclough was purposely framed in order to meet • elifilulty, because these pay- ments occasionally had to be mails at once or great inconvenience and possible loss would accrue to those Ito whom the accounts were due. (Hear, hear.) In any case, when that had to be done the accounts had to be passed by the Finance Committee, and they were sub- ' sevently brought before their own committee tsefore they were handed over to the Borough Treasurer for payment. The r3solution superseded the Standiag Order. Councillor DODDS sail his attent'on was not sailed to that resolution, so that he thought some apology was due to him. He woald not he a 'party to the Furnace Committee passing any account that had not use passed by the committee responsible. Alderman Sorroor mid he could Icily say the method adopted by the Finance Ceminittee was the method that bad been adopted ever since the beroueb was incor- porated, and it was the method adopted in every town and borough in Eigland. Councillor i eacmx : If I was a member of the Finance Co :mitres and I saw anytedne wrong I stolid I think it my duty to try and pat the committee rielet. But I wonld not, expose them outside first. (Applause, " Oh's " from the peblio and cries Of " Order.") Councillor DIDDS : tlay I exotain ? (Cries of " Chair " and" No no.") We discussed it for nearly an hour and the committee passed a resolution unanimously in my favo3r. (Loplatiate) Alderman M,elits said the payments, which hid given rise to that discassiee,were not accounts which were gen- erally understood by the word " account." 'nosy were not acsaur tt for goods supelied. They were paymenta concerning contracts that were being carried out by the respective contractors for work that had been aporoved iv the resoective committees of the Council. That in itself showed the exceptional nature of the circeeristencee and the arrangements made, and in his opinion was sufficient justificatioa for the Finance Committee and the Council passing each a resolution ta enable a diffi- culty to be get ever. What gave rice to it was a letter from a Wiewick Water Works Contractor. who threat- e_ seed to rake proceedings ;against the Corporation because the certificate he bad from tie architect was not paid upon presentation. It was well known that certificates issued be' the architect were payable on demand, and it was unreasonable to expect contractors to wait for the remise procedure of the Corporation to be gone through. There is a difference between accounts far goods, pay- ment for sorviees rendered, and cavnaents like these which were payment.' made Fir contract work which bad been passed be the Council. ' Couneiller PEHBERTON said this was all misleading. An unfair attick had beers made upon a member of he Ceuneil. According to the minutes they had a resolu- tion " That no or ier for the payment of accounts be signed until the accennta have been passed by the res.. eective.committaes." It was net only the centract accounts ; other amounts were not signed. (Hear. hear). It was ease enough to call a special meeting of the Finance Committee to meet an emergency. Things were carried on in a 110IP manner. There wets, he added, an account for £l3 for Mr Lonedin'e expenses in London which was net signed. (Cenncillor DODDS : " Hear, hear.") Clumiller CRCS said, as a member of the Finance romrnittee who was present at the meeting in qua he was quite in accer I with Couneillors Dodde and Pemberton. It was most irregular and unbuaineeslike for any Finance Committee to have bills sent them that had not been posed by the respective conenitpes. had netting to do with Councillor Dulls oration at the Parr Hall, but he supported him in the resolutioa he pronesed at the Finance Committee, whinh was carried without any opposition. (Rear, hear, and applause). The minutes were then pissed. THE OLD POLICE BUILDINCW SITE.

Honks, at the outset referred to the vote of thenke to the Mayor. There was no doubt, he said, that the success which attended the opening ceremony was largely due to the special efforts which the Mayor made in order to ensure that everything would pass off well, In regard to the appointment of a caretaker the committee had rather compro- mised matters. The man Graham who had been caretaker for some time at the School of Art, had d me the work extremely well and he had been ap- pointed to leak after the new Technical School. It was contemplated extending the schools and he thought it was not unlikely that he (the speaker) woul I shortly have to submit a resolgtion dealing with the matter. With referenee to the proposed appointment of a director of education,i the mintre alluding to the matter was a very c important one, as it marked a new departure in cianectiol with the management of the institution as a whole. The Alderman etplainel why the official was to be called director of education, and said the commit- tee had no deters, to be thought to be anticipating the Government Education Bill, and they had no idea or tie-ought of committing the Council in that respect, The appeiatment was ietendel to refer ex elasively to the whole of the elacstien which at present came under the control of the Council, and which was generally termed secondary elucetien, a term well understood and which had no connection with elementary education. A printed slip had been sent to each applicant for the ' position detailing the duties. It referred Specifically to etch department which was under the control of the Committee and there was no mention whatever of ele- mentary education with one exceptien,an I th et was the probable establishment of higher erode elementary schools. No steps were at present being taken with regard to the ristabliehment of the school so that the stetement of the duties could not he said to refer to elementary education at all The Canemittee bad carried on their work fir the past eleven years with Mr Madeloy as secretary. He had also delve what oreenizetion had been came oat up to the present time, but the work was growing in a wee which pointed to the desirability of a man giving the whole of his time eel attention to this work. (Rtar, hear). Mr Medley eerie] not sin teat, as he was librarian and curator, and it seemed necessary thet he should reeige his present position and make way for a new man. Tne cenemittee recognised the hard Work he had done and wished to express their appreciation of his services. klderman Menke went on to speak of the difficulty which had been caused by the unexpected resignation of Mr Hermit/on, the headmaster and prirmipil of the Pupil Teachers' Centre. The Technical Instruction Cern- mittee bad taken over the management of that centre, and by arrangement with the committee of the centre they took over the whole staff. Just at the time wheu the change Was envie Mr Dennigon resigned quite tines- pecteely and left the rterninitteco in rather an awkward predialment beeanee at tee moment they had no bead of the °mere. Mr Dermisee's salary was £220 a year. The school at present was being carried on I by the two assistant., Miss Warburton and kir Buxton, with the assistance of dlr Hall, one of the reechine staff of the Institute, on Saturday morning. The committee had to choose between filling up the vacancy and making that anointment or waiting until the new education authority was formed. The !est- eemed event would not come about for some time, yet gni it did not seem at all wise to leave the centre with- out someone in charge. They could, of course, have gone on comfortably for a time, but the diffiollty of a headmaster seemed to the committee to be insuperahle, and therefore they decided neon the new departure. They wentel a good man, as the position was likely to be an important one, and the Museum Committee ware enekiere lonial efforts to get the beet man available at the moment. The duties of the official would be to act as secretary of the Technical Instruction Committee and the work woold also embrace the anpervieton and nen- trol of the education given in the following re-Scheel of Art (115 students), Technical Institute (254). Pupil Teaehers' Centre (103), Cernmercial School (246), Con- ti-matt/a School (276). and University extension ieetures (150 teener, attendance), so that they had under their control 1,144 students. Six day shoots seat their eitls to the centre COP instruction in cookery, and they had something like 450 scholars from tee day schools r eteeivine the necessary tuition in cooking at the centres in the 011 Barracks in Museum-street. The change to the new school email shortly be made, amid then the Committee would be able to deal with an even larger number of schelere if the other schools wished Ce take elvantsge of the facilities offered. With regard to the financial question, it had been stated that they were going to apsoint another high salaried official, and that the town would he landed in a further exeencliture of £3OO ner annum. That was not true, because they had the £223 which had been hitherto paid to Dr Dennison and the £5O acid to Mr Madeley, making £270. The cost of the clerical work would be ab out the same, bet probably they would have to give a little aesistanno in regard to the education of puoii teachers, which would element perhans to £75, so that the total exiles:dime would not exceed at the out- Rale £lO9 Der rear more than it had hitherto ben RA had been told thee the amount offered was far too much, and that they could get a good man for a great deal less, but he ventured to doubt that. The position Was of such import ince that it would justify the Pro- posal of the committee in suggesting a salary of £3OO. (Rear, hear.) The responsibility would be great, and they would have to rely a great deal upon the director of education for information, and the arrangements of the classee so that there would be clashing whatever. He thought that if they could get the right man and with the new conditions under which the week was to be done, they would have such a large increase lc the number of students and so much larger grants pate by the Government for better work done, that the additional income which would accrue would be far in excises of the £lOO a year which they proposed to pay in salaries. There was another way in which the success of the institutioe could be increased and that was by employers exercisine a little pressure on these in their service and by encouraging them te take advantage of the clatses which were pro- vided. Two employers had already set a good example by seeing that the boys and young people attended regularly, and if they attended, their face were returned at the end of the session, me a sort of reward and enceeragement• (Hear, hear.) Another firm had eetah'ished a scholarship in teepee] to its own particular industry to encoursee its workpeople to study the tschnicalities of the trades. As regarded the OXDondl- two as a whole, last year seneunte I to about £2,600. They started the year with a leficit of £lOO nod finiseed with a balance in heed of £234 so that they kept the expenditure wi-hin the income which the Corporation provided for them. Daring the current year the ex- penditure and the income would be more. As far as he herl been able to estimate it, the amount cretin be £3,000 and that would enable the committee to carry on the Magpie without asking for more money except in , regard to interest and sinking fund on the new buildtng. If the Corporation would undertake those charge. the eemmittee weeld be well satisfied and could manage without snaking any further call on the Council. He would like to mention that in many towns the buildings were provided by private individuale and therefore the teem was saved the interest and sinking fund charges. When it was de- cided to erect the schools ha Warrington the committee thought it would he a rather nice thing if they could get them paid for,without having to come before the Council for the necessary money. A circular, signed by the Mayor for the time being, was sent to all large employ- ers and a nurnler of leading men of the town, asking them if they would do anything towards nesting for the building. The committee wanted £15,000, and they thought it was no use making a nubile appeal for money nnless they had a promising stare Phey thought teat if they could get promises sof subscriptions from those people wile might fairly be expected to take an interest jul the institution it wou'd be a very gee I thing. He was able to secure two premieres of £l,OOO each before sending out the circulate. Uefortunately the circulars met wits no favourable response whatever, and it was necessary to drop the thing and let it go through as it had done, and become at charge upon the rates. Oen firm promised to do Something if the matter was generally taken up, and the two promises that he (Alderman Monks) obtained were couditional. div.p: OLD AND NEW WAYS OF TREATING DEAFNESS.

After reading the latest issue of the " Imes! for the Deaf." there at once occurs a train of theught leading one to wonder why doctors still persist, in using the old method of treating deafness, by torturing their patients with instruments, air-pumps, and operative procedures, when there exists an infinitely superior, as well as a miler wiy, the Drotiet treatment. The principles of this latter method, which consists chiefly of a local application behind the ear, are given very completely in the Journal, together with a series of cured cases illus- trating its success in the most obstinate forms of deafness —in faot, in those previously considered incurable. div.head: HOSPITAL SUNDAY.
div.p: HOSPITAL SUNDAY.

A meeting of the Hospital Sunday Committee was beld in the Board Room at the Infirmary yesterday afternoon. Mr John Faircloagh, JP. was voted to the chair, and there were also present: The Revs E C E Carleton, W Bracecamp, John Yonge, Fathers Whittle and Ryan, Mr T Birchall, Mr John Coxon, Mr A J Jolley (hon secretary of the Hospital Sun- day Committee),and Mr J H J Hampson (secretary to the Infirmary. In submitting his annual report, Mr A J JOLLY said three places of worship which contributed to the Hospital Sunday Fund in 1901 failed to do so in 1902. Five commenced or renewed their contribu- tions. On balance there was a net gain of .£3 us 6d under these heads. The total receipts have been £326 18s 21, an increase over last year of .31 6s 74. Of this amount £2ll 18s ai was collected within and .£ll4 19s 6d outside the Borough. The expenses of the .fund were £l6 lOs as compared with .£l5 in 1901. The report was adopted, Mr A J Jolley was re- elected hon secretary to the committee and thanked for his past servics. In acknowledging the compliment, Mr Jolley said it was some satisfaction to feel that during the ten years he had held the position of hon sec- etary there had been a steady increase in the mount collected, and he hoped it would continue the future. (Hear, hear.) It was decided that March 15th, 1903 be the date the next Hospital Sunday. be meeting terminatsd with an acknowledgment the Chairman's services

WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
Mr. Charles E. Parker on "America,"
A Contrast in Educational Systems.

The monthly " Club eight " in connection with the Warrington Society was held on Th ursday last Week at the Old Academy,Mr Charles E Parker delivering a lecture on ' America." There was a good attendance and the lecturer's interesting, picturesque, and at times, exciting story was appreciatively listened to. The chair was occupied by Mr J Fulton Smith At the outset Mr Psrk,r contrasted the educational systems of America and this ceuntr. In doing so, he said that the strik*ne feature about the American Educational System was the lack of system. In America there was 'Telly no national system, each State, each eity,and each district working out its own system. There had been no eaiting fcr, and no depending upon State authority and State con- trol. And so they had in the States an infinite variety of educational methods, an uneven progress, and a striking lack of symmetry. flare they saw the great difference between the American and the Continental systems, say those of France and Germany. In those ceuntries the control, direction, supervision, initiative, all came from the central authority in Paris or Berlin. In America the control was located in the town, county, or individual State. The English system came between the American and Cocitinental. With us the direction and control of education was partly local and partly national, The E'ucational Authority at Washington correeponded with that of England, only in so far as it tollectea esetistles and die'rdeeted lefortustion ; it exercised no controlling inflect:We Mr the eilueetiell in the States or localities. These were all left to devise their own methods and to work out their own systems. In a numbsr of cities and districts the educatienai authority was appointed by the Mayor, or by the 11 Ivor and City Council acting together. In others the election was directly by vote sf the people, To ileastrate the Manner of appointment he would instance the Milwaukee method of running the educational machinery. The people elected the Mayor, the Mayor appointed the Commission, the Commission appointed the Board, the Board eletted the Superintendent, the Super- intendent elected the Principals, the Prin- cipals selected the teachers, and the t e,achers taught the schools. This was a very exceptional case, but It served to illustrate the variety ef methods of appointment. Lake all American pylitical affairs, the appointment Of th.e. Educational Authority was not forto from the 919119 s habit which accompanied change of party. The principle of ss the spoils to the victors " was specially injurioue to a continuity of educational preerses. If a change of party Cameinto the Council, the whole of the officials were otter chanced, including those who bad control of edueatioe. There was area- lug in the S.atea a strong feeling ageonet that, and earnest endeaveurs were being made to remove educa- tion out of tee reach of popular caprice and change. In come/el:le the educational results with their own they bad to take into aceciant the widely different conditions which existed in the States,, compared with those in England. If theV contrasted the education, say in the State of Massechusette with that of England,they woula probably Come to the conclusion that both in equip- ment and in result irs was eenciderab!se ahead of that in England ; if on the feller hand they took one cf the Southern States, touch al South Carolina, where the negro penulation formed eueh a large proportion, they would fled the education much inferior. In Mas- eacnusetts, the amount goent per child was V 103. Per annum, while in South Care9nait wee only 16s. The average for the whole of the United States was 76e The average in Germane wee 33a,. Franco 375, In Eopland 41s 71. So the Arner'eans spent nearly twice as much on the edunatien of each child as the English did ; this might in part he accounted for by the higher cost of earine. In 30 States thee load cemeulsory attendance IaWB, while in 16 States there was no law on the sutject. 11" "'ne if compulsory attendance in most qtates was 5 to 14, hut that also varied nsiderably. In North Carolina the average number of days that the rralaiia (moiled on the co books attended the echeels in 1899 was 36.3 while in Massachusette the numeer was 143 5. The resiaber of days the schnote were itoe aCr,i,nd 143. seeile

in England, France and Germany, the number was abut 200. Tbe average in the States was brought down by the sparsely populated and poor farm ling districts many of which had only a winter school- session. In North Carolina the schools were only open 68 days in the year. MI public primary schools, a large portion of public secondary schools, and nearly all State Universities were free. In regard to the means of rais- ing the funds, the following were the sources of revenue .—From rents from land given by the Govern- ment, 4.4 per cent. ; from State taxes, 17.7 per cent. ; from local sources, 70 3 per cent. ; tram other sources, 76 pet cent ; total, 1000. Those were average figures and would vary in each State and locality. For example in the ety of Omaha half the school revenue was derived from saloon licences. He had given them a few facts from which they would gather that as far as the framework of the education system was connerned,:it was not in any way in advance of the,r owe. Wherein he was confident that America excels Us not so much in the educational machinery as the spirit in which that machinery was worked. It had been truly said that American common peeple believed in the school while the European, including the English common people, only tolerated them. It was that indifference of the English democracy to t educa- tional efficiency for the children that was the despair of every good educationalist. There was a great deal they could learn from America, and one of the most impor- tant lessons was how to infuse their countrymen with the enthusiasm the Americans had for that knowledge which was power and strength and life.

Dedication of the New Organ.

_ Thursday last week witnessed an interesting event in the history of Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. Great improvements have been effected of late in the interiot of the building, and the most important has been the entire re-construction of the organ. This work has been very satisfactorily carried out by Mr A Caldwsll, of at. Helens, who has engaged in similar undertakings in various Lancashire towns. Parts of the old organ have been utilized in the re-construction, but the instrument is now considerably larger than it was before. fhe total number of pipes is 1,032, and of these about 300 were in use in the old organ. The swell organ contains ten stops with 548 pipes, the great organ eight stops with 424 pipes, and the pedal organ two stops with 60 pipes. There are three couplers and six composition pedals. The organ case is of pitch pine, varnished, and the pipes are taeefully de- corated in blue and gold. The instrument is pneumatic, and will be blown by an electric motor. In addition to the re-construction of the organ, several improvements which were included in the original scheme of re-decoration have been com- pleted. The appearance of the church has been much improved hy the artistic stencilling round the gallery and new curtains have been introduced in the choir gallery. The rostrum has been newly upholstered and the reading desk suitably draped. The aisles have been covered with cork linoleum. A new system of lighting is at present under con- sideration.

A service for the dedication of the new organ was held on Thursday last :week, and was well attended. The preacher was the Rev T Haidw.ek Mawson,o' Altrn- cham, who was accompanied on the rostrum by the Rev G H Carnson (superintendent of the circuit) and the Revit Wilkins Rees (minister-in-charge ef the church). The preacher based a powerful discourse on the words "And He built His sanctuary like high palaces " (Psalm 78, verse 69.) A collection was taken on behalf of the organ fund and rcalind £l3 At the conclusion of the service an organ recital was given by Mr E Heywood,A.R.C.O.,of St Helens,who dis- played great ability and brought out the full powers of the instrument. The pieces rendered were:—Sonata in D minor (Gustav Merkel) ; Toccata in E flat (P Capecci) ; Allegretto in B minor (Alex Guilmanc). MB. C. E. PARKER AND CHURCH MUSIC.

In the evening Mr Heywood gave another recital. There was a good attendance, Mr C E Parker presiding. The Rev R WILKINS REES said the amount yet to ho raised to pay for the improvements was about £4OO. He appealed to those present to contribute liberally towards that sum. There was also a trust debt of sem, thing like £lOO, the income of the church in con- nection with trust purposes being insufficient to cover the annual expenditure. LI concluiion dlr. Rees ox- pressed his great pleasure at the presence of Mr Parker. The CHAIRMAN said he was very pleased to he associ- ated with them in connection with the effort they were making to improve their Church services. There was considerable need that they, as Weslevans, should turn their attention to making their services as attractive and pleasant, and as great a power for gcod,as possible. Perhaps in the past they had trusted to the sermon too much, as if that were the only thing of importance in the service, and the rest did nr t matter. He was not quite sure that they did not have too much sermonising. If they could only carry into action one tenth of the good things which they heard from the ralpit, they would do well. In regard to the development of the musical part of the services, he would have the friends who had charge of it, remember that the bulk cf Methodist congregations were composed very largely, almost entirely, of the work- ing class population. He hoped it would ever be so, for the mission of Methodism, the genius of Methodism, the whole spirit and tone of Methedism,was adapted to the masses. Those of them who were woi k- ing people had not very much opportunity, facility, or imagination, to cultivate that high-class musical intelligence which their musical friends possessed, and he hoped that however far they developed the musical service at Heavy-road, they would never develop it so far that there would be in the congregation a great many who began to feel that they bad no part or lot in the matter. (Hear, hear). There might be something to be said equally on the other side. He did not know about Bewsey-road, but people who had spoken to him about the develop- ment of the musical service had said they did ' not believe in these new fangled notions. They did not believe in chants, psalms, and part singing, because they never knew " where they came in." ,What they liked was a real good old Methodist tune,witb everybody singing and making noise enough to nearly lift the roof, and they protested very loudly against the improvement of the musical service. It seemed to him that there were two exttemes to guard against. They could never get a cengregation all of the same mind, and what they needed in this, as in all branches of the work of the Christian Church, was that they snoula ••in ROI:Wm prof, .no another." In so far as they developed and cultivated thst spirit of self-sacrifice, upon which lay the very root and I.sis of the Christian faith, the more would their churches and chapels become united and strong, and they would work together for the benefit of those around them and ir the glory of their God and Christ. div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE
SOCIETY.

In connection with the above a temperance meet- ing was held on Monday evening in the Camden Wesleyan Church, Runcorn. Councillor Davies, of Widnes, presided, and wad supported on the plat- form by the Revs A Wells (superintendent minister) and J B Foster and Messrs J Allen (Liverpool), E Marsnall, D Bisbrown, T Cooke, S Coventry, J Bellamy, L Rosenberg, jun.. T Leach, J Anders, G Littler, S Littler and S C Beckett. The Rev I B Foster read the report. He said amid the many societies and other operations of the present day, temperance work was crowded into a corner. But they were convinced that the leaven had been working silently through the year, and in accordance with a suggestion of the District Tem- perance Committee they on Sunday made an effort to discover their strength in all the congregations ar.d schools of the circuit. Slips were provided so that all whe were interested in temperance work in the sense of being total abstainers might let them know of their sympathy. The result was immensely encouraging. It was the best tonic he had had for a long time. In connection with St Paul's and Brunswick School 278 signed the declaration that they were total abstainers and 14 ,igned the pledge for the first time. At Halton- toad the figures were 64 total abstainers and one new pledge ; Camden, 146 and 17; Halton, 121, and one; Preston Brook, 39 and one; Weston, 81 and one ; Weston Paint, 47. (Applause.) They were assured out of congregations on Sunday which were somewhat less than ordinary that there were 776 loyal abstainers, while 25 took the pledge. (Ap• plause ) If possible the foltowing figures were even more encouraging. The statistics were gathered from the Sunday schools on Sunday. In all the achoolq there were 95 teachers, and out of them 88 declared tnemselves to•al abstainers._ There were

1,043 childrfa in this scL)ol, and 991 were total abstainers. Of those 376 were under 14 years of age and 415 were over that age. lie was proud to say that Camden led the:my in the matter of the schools with 129 over 14 years of age, who were total ebstainers and Brunswick made a good second with 98 (Applause.) They must c3nsiler this report etninewly satisfactory. He only hoped the few teachers who were not yet on the right side would speedily join the great art.), and throw in their l,t with there. (Applause.) The Chairman alluding :o the deaths of the Ray

Hugh Price Hughes and Dr Parker, hoped that the mitaatle of these godly men would fall upon young, .eoucated,and enthusiastic -Len all over the country. ,(Applause) He had Lime sympathy with the publican, but he had no sympathy with clubs and „grocers licences. He considered that the publicans' licences should be redueed ,by half. He thought there were signs all reund of aa advance being made. He referred with satisfaction to the forth- coming police supervision over clubs, which latter be stronely condemned as bringing about the ruin of theueands of young men. Re advocated educa- tion work among tee younz, and urged Sueday echool teachere to exert an inuance for good in this metter upon the children. (Applause.) Mr Allen delivered a general neeress upon the temperance geestion. alluded with eatisfac- tion to the stand the Methodist Chureli had taken in regard to temperance, and advocated agitation, .oducatiou, and legislation His programme was Sunday closing,a reduction of the number of public houses without compensation. a curtailing of hours, a ra'sing of the age under whicn children should int be served, the abolition of grocers' ecences,and a better regulation of clubs (Apoleuse.) He trusted that wen the war and the Education gill were out of the way they weule demand legislation upon temperance lines, and if the Churches iasisted upon i,,it, might very easily be carried out. (Ap- plause ) A c election was taken and was followed by other speech-is. Several musical items and a recitation were also contributed.

div.p: tettero to tbe Ebitor.
The Recent Eisteddfod.

should like to trespass on your valuable space for a few momtnts to make a few remarks concerning the Male Voice Choir Competition at the recent :Eisteddfod in Warrington promoted by the Apollo Mee Voice Choir. lam not going to bemoan the 12013-9110Cess of my choir but I wish to mention one er two reasone, why we did not win or rather why we did not gain a higher place on the lint. The prize was awarded to Ruoeorn whereas the real winners were Runcorn and St Helens combined, as the former their bad the assistance of at least half a dozen members of the latter choir. Also I observed that a few of the Wigan Harmonic singtrs, sang with the Makerfield choir. Now I contend that such is not fair fighting. If Runcorn choir Inter. then let it be Runcorn and not them and some one else ; and the same in respect to Makerfield. At these choir competitions, the choirs should, in my opinion, coneist of bona-fide members and nc4 be collected from different choirsin en-irely different towns. I for one strongly object to compete when such condi- tions exist especially where the feet is omitted from the official programme. I don't believe in entering these musical competitions just simply to swell the entrance fees,to make the conaern pay,or to gala the money prize offered. .

The conducter printed on the programme to lead Runcorn was Mr J Brown. The St Helens choir (con- ductor Mr Ei Berrey), did not Out in an appearance as separate compatito-s but the Runcorn conductor was superseded by Mr Berrey. There is a note on the Eisteddfod programme to this effect " That no members of the Apollo Clink will be allowed to assist other choirs." Is not Mr H Berrey who is conductor af the Apollo a member P Thanking you in anticipation of insertiog this letter, Yours truly, W. H. PA.YTON.

Sir,—ln your last issue I oleic() your request "Per- haps Mr Nayler will take us iato his confidence." Now resprotine tee Longford Der I have only mentioned this on the occasions when addressing =stings of the Non-Trading Association." Ist. I made the distinct statement—l b lieved the Der 6: had mit an excessive amount, and I would hire the ratepayers to be informed of the amount, and cam- pers the same with its actual present value after making due allowance for depreciation. This seems gusto a fair thing for any ratepayer to ask, and I should be glad if the proper authorities would pnblicly state this. 2nd. At the last meeting I stated, what I believed to be a fact, that costly experiments have been made at the Depot at the ratepayers' expense for which no value has been received. _ _ _
This irstormation I had, in the first instance, from a member of a certain deputation who visited the place from North Lancashire.

I have sines made inquiries in Warrington from gentlemen who emrlat to know and I understand the expenditure of the Longford Depot has been the talk of the town for years. Without the proof is forthclinirrg to the contrary I shall still maintain that this branch nf Corporation enterprise has certainly not been con- ducted in accordance with the best interests of the ratepayers. As regards the smell creatsd we seem to be quite agreed for it certainly does bear some kinship to that which has driven me from hoine,but very very stight,as it would take several Lnegford to create a nnis- once bringing in Ai train such alarming effects. Yours truly, R. A. NAYLOR. St AUchsels' Rouse. Egerton Gardens, S.W. December sth 1901. Councillor F. R. Roberts and the Library.

Sir,—At the last Council naeesing, Councillor F. R Roberts made a statement on the Library question. This is distinctly a good site. Some of us have been asking for reform, belt hitherto the people in the castle have scarcely deigned to admit their knowledge that we were knocking at the gate. At last perseverance is rewarded, and a Geuneillor has replied, I trust you will allow me space for a rejoinder. The Councillor says he does not know my qualifications to speak on the cob- ject, but why limit the issue P It is not Roberts v. Hulme, but Roberts V. malty diseatisfied ratepayers, and my individual quelificatiens do not therefore greatly matter. With some justice I mieht question his qualie- fication to reply, as durine the last municipal year, be did not attend a single meeting of the Museum (end Library) Committee. It seems fairies clear from this that he is not much concerned whether the Library rives or does not provide what the people want. It is, disappointing when a counsellor who does not attend his II committee meetings will accept no scilicet from out-1 eiders who at least take an interest in the Library, and wish to see it improved. Why does he make his base- less assertion that my only object is to " malign the Couacil." That sweet morsel •ss native and imported maligaity " seems to have taken a permanent hold on the minds of some of our eouncillors, and unless critic- ism is favenrable it must be denounced as malignant. Let me assure him he is on the wrong tack. have no desire to hurt sr malign anyboiy,but simply wish to see a better Library in Warrington, and there is surely mach room for improvement. Conneillor FR Roberta' eeasensent in the Ceuncil left the real question quite untouched. Be said they had purchased c-rtein books this month, the titles of which he read our. Thin list notwithstanding, I repeat now that taking one list with another we have not an alsqnate supply of modern fiction in the library. It is easy to take a particular list and say it is " one month's purchases," but by comparing his list with any ordinary quarterly list, it can be seen that the former is exceotionally fey- ourable, and by no means representative of the regular putclemes. Let any unprejudiced person go to the library and see the lists pinned on the board there. They are vary dirty, and look as though disinfecting would improve them, but they show the additions in fiction over the year Ootober IS9I to September 1892 to have been about 180 volumes of which 39 are classed as juvenile, being a special purehme to make up the lee- way in that clam We have thus some 140 new volumee in a year to satisfy a demand fr fiotion,of pr ,bably 200 borrowers a day on the average, so that calculating lac seven days for reading, a harrower may expect a new book every nine or ten weeks—say fiVi nr six in a year. It must be remembered that these so-celled new books are by no means newly published in many cases ; in the wnrl4 of books they are often a year or two old before they can be found on the shelves of our Free Library. Taking these books on their merits however, I do not hesitate to say that they ere not the " cream of English novel literature," and I suggest as a mere tppropri ate term " skim milk with an occasional splash of cream." In eeee of the fare-going fleerea, the councillor's state- ment that " month by month " such purchases as he named were made is csttainly misleading and indeed incorrect. I will not sconce him of deliberate mierepresentatinn, is I think it trite likely that his long absence from the Museum Committee meetings may ac- count for his mistake and I wish to be as charitable as he eine had the repAetion of being. The real point however, is not whether 10, 20 or 30 books were bought in some psricular pvriod, hut whether the normal supply is adequate. My contention is that it is absurd to go to the expense of rent and salaries if, after these are paid, we cannot have a satie- factory and regular supply of current literature, and further, that leas sxmoditure on the Museum and a corresponding addition to the book fund weuld be mere satisfactory to the great majority of the nuelee Thie the councillor nays nettling about. and if I have heard cerrectly, be himself has been knowe to egeress the view that the Library is neelectel as compared with the Museum. He said nothing about the miesing Library report ; nothing about the long-waited-for catalogue. Can the committee justify their own nerrleet in not see- ing that the catalogue Was published years ago 1 At Parr Hall, Councillor Union referred to branch libraries ; his boldness almost toek my breath away, but I suppees we shall have these some day. Have the committee con- sidered the question ? There are other points I easel raised before. Will Councillor F R Roberts say when proper accommodation for ladies new be expeetee at the Library, and when the claims of the children will be taken in'e censideratinn.? In a word, if we are to he favoured with official 'netts and replies, let them cover the whole ground, ins, teed of a single point only, and even that incorrectly and improperly dealt with. It is no use telling us that a dozen good books have just been bought. We want to handle such books fairly regularly and we cannot. If Clunciller Roberts were one of the public with no special access to the books, he would find it very difficult indeed to get any satisfaction out of the Library, for the simple reason that the supply of new books is insufficient. Our municipal enterprise, in fact. is plot to shame by the activity of our Private Circulat- leg Libraries, to wnich many who have the right to de- mand better thine of the Free Library have been driven —Yours teuly, ALFRED HOWSE. Fairfield-read, Latchford.

div.head: "GREEN DRAGON" LICENCE.
div.p: THE "GREEN DRAGON" LICENCE.
Second Application for a Transfer Refused. -- Interesting Evidence.

A second application for the transfer of the licence of the" Green Dragon" Inn, Bridge-street, to a private residence known as " The Brooklands," Lovely-lane, came before the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday. Mr Rigby Swift, barrister (instructed by Messrs A Browne andgromoton) appeared on behalf of the applicant, and Mr F Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr T S Steel) opposed the application. The magistrates on the Bench were 7—Mr John Fairclough presid- ing, Aldermen James Fairclough, FrancomleHeaton, and Sutton, Dr Fox, and Messrs S Wright, J W Hayward, T Birchall, R T Fairclough, E J Guest and H Tnornton. Great interest centred in the application and there was a large attendance of the general public. Mr Rigby SwifS said he was instructed to apply on behalf of James Spencer Earle, who was at pre- sent the licensee of the "Green Dragon," Bridge. street, to grant him a licence to carry on business at a house known as "The Brooklands," in Lovely- lane. It might be within the knowledge of some of their worships that he made a similar application on the 6th of October, and on that occasion the Bench intimated that they were not prepared ta grant it, and it, was therefore di-naimsed. At the same time some remark fell from the Bench about the matter requiring further consideration, and although at the time he (Mr Swift) intimated that his clients would in all probability appeal, he gave that intimation rateer in his position as an advocate than as having any specific instructions upon the point. After his clients had consulted ' among themselves tney came to the conclusion, which he ventured to think was a right one, that in a matter of that kind the local Bench were the proper people to deal with it, and they ought not to go above their worships and ask any other Court to deal with matters which were particularly matters for the consideration of the Bench. Consequently, instead of going to the Qearter Sessions, they came to the conclusion that the proper course Was to again lay the facts before the Bench and ask them to say, on further consideration, that the applica- tion was a proper one and one which ought to be granted. Mr James Spencer Earle had for three years been the licensee of the Green Dragon, and for a considerable time the Corporation had been widening Bridge-street. The improvements had now reached that stage that it had become neces- sary for the Corporation to deal with the Green Dragon. They had power under their Act to take down the whole of the front of Bridge-street, and it was necessary from all practical points of view of business and even municipal government that the people who were dispossessed of their premises— many of whom had old-established businesses— should be supplied with other premises as nearly as possible in the same place. The Corporation found that in order to rebuild Bridge-street an the new building line so as to reinstate all those who were dispossessed by the improvements it would be necessary to entirely abolish the Green Dragon, Consequently, the Corporation, in the first instance, and the Corporation throughout bad approached Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Co, the owners, and asked them to find suitable premises to submit to , the magistrates as convenient for the licence to be ' transferred to. The company had consequently acquired premises in Lovely-lane known as 'The Brooklaade." It was proposed, with the permission of the Bench, to transfer the licence to Bro klands. and althoughthe application was made in Mr Earle's name, he would ask the Bench to observe that it was made at the instance of the Corporation. Although he would not suggest for a moment that "The Brooklands" was more convenient to the Corporation than any other place they had been able to find,it was the best place from the point of view of Messrs Greenall and Whitley, and, he should sub- mit, the best place for the licence to:be removed to in the public interests Of Mr Earle's good char- acter there could be no question, indeel he would receive the highest character from tlie Chief Om- steble. He felt sure there would not be any dispute as to the fitness of the house, which was built about 30 years ago by Mr Monks as a private resid- ence, butewith the slightest alterations practically no alteration at all, it would be admirably suited for the purpose to which it was proposed to put it. He unhesitatingly eubmitted that if any licences were to be granted anywhere this was a neighbour- hood in which there ought to be a licence. There were people who appeared to think that no licence ought to be granted under any circumstances, but that was not the view the Legislature adopted, and he was quite sure it was the view which would be adopted by any member of a Bench which eat for the purpose of granting licences. It would be ridiculous for a body to adjudicate upon a question of granting or refusing licences, if they came with the determination that no licences were required at all. The Legislature contempla- ted that licences would be required, and the justices had to determine where any particular licences were to be granted. He submitted that the neighbourhood in question was one which particularly required a licensed house. In no other part of War :ngton, be was instructed. could such a state of things be found as existed in the neighbourhood of Lovely-lane Within a:radius of 400 yards frons"The Brooklands' there were in the year 1890 429 houses, which gave at the ordinary rape of computation,a poouletion of 2,248. Since 1890 there had been built 367 houses, making a total of 796 houses with a population of 4,171. The population was Increasing and a great number of the new houses had been built quite re- cently. Building operations were still going on, and within the quarter of a mile radius for the benefit of the 4,171 people there was not a solitary fuliy - licensed public - house There was one off-beer licence,but the nearest fully. licensed public-house was the Railway Hotel in Priestley-street, and it was 743 yards away. Such a thing was not to be found anywhere else in the borough and it was unreasonable to say that a neighbourhood like that did not require a public- house if any neighbourhood in the world required one. Continuing, he contended that the Bench were not present to listen to the whims and fancies of particular individual+, whether they wanted the house or did not, but what was for the benefit and in the interests of the whole community. Since the last application was merle to the Court teens hadbeen a good deal of agitation in certain quarters and amongst certain people against the grant- ,ling of the licence to Lovely-lane, but such an I agitation and MCI an interference with their worship's discharee of their duty was an impertin- ence. At the same time he was bound to notice that impertinence lest any of their worships might be inclined to attach weight to what was said or done at the meeting in qusstion. He was confident that what he asked would be acceded to,and that the Bsnch would not allow any agitation, or anything done at meetings where per. eons were imported from Manchester—(laughter)— or any other piece in order to denounce their wor- ship's action to influence them. He asked the Bench not to notice such meetings or each agitation, but te dissharge the duty which the Legislature had imposed on them, and which the courts had said quite recently was their duty to consider for them- selves, namely, the wants and interests of a par- ticular neighbourhoo I. They should bring their knowledge of a particular neighbourhood to bear and act as they believed in the public interests. He did not propose to call any evidence unless any par- ticular points were asked for by the Bench. The Borough Surveyor, the architect,and Mr Earle were present and they would be glad to answer any question that, might be put by the Bench. The Town Clerk was also present on behalf of the Im- provement Committee of the Corporation, and was instructed to support the application. Mr Thornton aultPd what was the dietaries from Market-gate to tag " Green Drava " opening. div.head: ST. HELENS SHOOTING TRAGEDY. --- Murder Trial at Liverpool.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS SHOOTING TRAGEDY. --- Murder Trial at Liverpool.
Shaw Acquitted.

Wednesday at Liverpool A.94iZi9 wss R 1703 up principally to the trial of the alleged :it. Helens. homicide, James ';haw (43), collier, who was in- dicted for the wilful murder of Michas! Noonan on, August sth. Both men were colliers. They and other friends had been drinking in the Boilermakers' Arms Noonan left to go home, and was followed by prisoner and his friends. A quarrel between them. ensued,and in tne fighting that took place Shawwn alleged to have shot Noonan fatally in the stomach. He pleaded that he had no intention to shoot Noonan ; he had a gun in his hand, the trigger of which was knocked by someone in the crowd, and/ so caused the weapon to go off. Alfred Ashton, who was in company with the Noonan party, said he saw Shaw put his head into the inside of his coat pocket, and get the gun. He fired it at a distance of two yards from the deceased The gun was not fired in the air. Witness did not hear any of them say to Shaw, "We'll have thee.and thy— —gun too." It was not true that the gun want off in the struggle. Thomas Noonan, orother of the deceased, cor- roborated. Alter he had shot witness's brother. prisoner said : " I will go and g3t another gun if no is not finished. I will blow all your brains out." •

div.head: Mr Tobin,.K.C., and Mr Leslie Scott_ conducted
div.p: Mr Tobin,.K.C., and Mr Leslie Scott_ conducted

the prosecution, and Mr Rigby Swat defended. The case had not concluded when the court rose, and the jury were locked up for the night on the premises. On Thursday Mr Swift submitted to the jury. on prisoner's behalf that the Normans and Aehtons had gone out of their way to the extent of a quarter of a mils to meet with Shaw, who was the only one of the other party upon whom they bad not wreaked vengeance for a previous quarrel, with the view of havinz a row. They went in the direction in which he had gone. It was a reasonable thing that Shaw, who wee in the habit of going out in the pursuit of game, snotild csrry a gun in his pocket, but there was no suggestion of provocation which should in- duce Shaw to fire at Noonan. Counsel went on to comment on the disparity between the witnesses as to the number of shots fired. Two witnesses swore only one shot was tired, whilst the prosecution ac- cepted the evidence of all the rest of the witnesses that two shots were fired. It had beea pointed out that there were alternative verdicts wnich the jury might return—murder, manslaughter, or acquittal. The poteibility of a verdict of wilful murder had been swept aside,and if it were accepted that the prisoner was only endeavouring to retain his gun he was doing a lawful act, and the result was not manslaughter but accident. The Judge, in summing up, said the theory of the prosecution was that during the time the fight was going on near Twist's house, prisoner dis- appeared, and was away long enough to go home and get his gun. If that theory had been suffici- ently established to their mind it was a very I material point. if they thought the men had met and during a struggle the gun bad gone off as had been stated by the defence, then they must treat it as an accident. Whatever they did they must arrive at a unanimous verdict. It had to be made clear beyond a reasonable doubt. He hoped they would arrive at a verdict in accordance with their conscience, and if they did that everybodp would have to be satisfied.

At the cpnclu4on of his lorthhip's address, he WII3 requested by the jury to ask Thomas Noonan and Allred Ashton if thoy understood the serious- ness of giving false evidence. Both men replied in the affirmative.
The jury then retired, THE VERDICT.
After an abeence of nearly an hour, the jury returned, and asked if they were agreed. ,The Foreman replied that they were, and found tie prisoner " Not guilty." Shaw was thereupon discharged.
